albania.name: Albania
albania.intro: Europe's last-discovered 'hidden gem', and the wonder nation that shielded Jews through its moral code of 'Besa' (the pledge of honor).
history: Albania is a country of extraordinary intrigue in Europe, full of 'mystery' and dramatic contrasts. Due to its particular history and geography, its image in the eyes of Western Europeans is unusually complex — burdened with lingering stereotypes of 'gangsters' and 'danger', yet continually re-understood through the hard work of its construction workers and, in recent years, its 'affordable paradise' coastline.

In language and faith, Albania is likewise an 'outlier': Albanian is completely isolated within the Indo-European family, with no close relatives; and although it has traditionally been a Muslim-majority country (a legacy of the Ottoman Empire), it became extremely secular after long decades of radical atheist rule — Western Europeans are often surprised by its 'secular Muslim culture of beer-drinking and pork-eating'.

World War II is a frequently overlooked highlight of Albanian history. In 1939 it was annexed by Italy, and after Italy's surrender in 1943 it was occupied by Nazi Germany; yet it accomplished a miracle — becoming the only country in postwar Europe whose Jewish population rose rather than fell (from roughly 200 before the war to more than 2,000 after it). This stemmed from its deeply rooted moral law of 'Besa' (keeping one's promise): once someone seeks refuge in your home, your home belongs to that guest and to God, and the host is even willing to protect them with his life. During the Nazi occupation, almost none of the Jews sheltering there were ever handed over.

After the war, Albania swung to the other extreme: Enver Hoxha established an iron-fisted regime, falling out successively with the West, the Soviet Union and even China, becoming a completely isolated 'North Korea of Europe'. Convinced that World War III was imminent, he ordered the construction of as many as 170,000 concrete bunkers nationwide — to this day, beaches, hillsides and residential areas remain dotted with these mushroom-like bunkers, forming the country's most absurd yet most distinctive landscape.
music: Albania's classical music may be less celebrated than that of the established Western European nations, yet it has nurtured numerous internationally renowned artists in vocal music (especially opera) and strings. Its folk tradition is equally deep-rooted, and the 'Iso-polyphony' of the south has been inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

musicians.name: Inva Mula
musicians.desc: A world-renowned soprano; the label most familiar to the public is the aria of the alien blue diva in the sci-fi film The Fifth Element — the dazzling coloratura spanning an enormous vocal range — which she performed behind the scenes.

musicians.name: Ermonela Jaho
musicians.desc: One of the leading sopranos of our time, known for her dramatic intensity and emotional penetration; a regular at the Royal Opera House in London and the Metropolitan in New York, and widely regarded as one of the finest interpreters of Puccini (such as Madama Butterfly) today.

musicians.name: Saimir Pirgu
musicians.desc: An internationally acclaimed tenor, admired and mentored by the king of tenors, Pavarotti, and active on the world's great opera stages.

musicians.name: Tedi Papavrami
musicians.desc: A world-class violinist who rose to fame as a child prodigy, later trained in France, and established himself in the classical world through superb technique and profound interpretations of Paganini.

musicians.name: Çesk Zadeja
musicians.desc: Hailed as the 'father of Albanian classical music', he combined rich folk elements with symphonic structure, laying the foundation for the country's modern classical music.

radios.name: Radio Tirana 3 (RTSH Klasik)
radios.note: The official classical channel of Albanian Radio Television (RTSH), an excellent window onto the little-known classical music of the Balkans.

radios.name: Radio Tirana 1
radios.note: RTSH's main channel, airing a great deal of Albanian folk and traditional music.

andorra.name: Andorra
andorra.intro: A tiny Pyrenean principality famed for duty-free shopping, where music is a meeting point of Catalan, French and Spanish cultures.
history: Andorra is one of Europe's oldest principalities, governed since 1278 jointly by the Bishop of Urgell in Spain and the President of France (historically the King of France) — a curious 'dual head of state' system that endures to this day. Nestled in the Pyrenees, it is one of Europe's smallest and highest-altitude countries.

Sealed off by mountains, Andorra long relied on agriculture and herding, then grew rapidly wealthy in the 20th century through skiing and duty-free shopping. With only about 80,000 inhabitants, it is nonetheless one of Europe's most tourist-dense nations.
music: Andorra's music is deeply rooted in Catalan tradition: Catalan folk songs (such as the havanera), the Sardana circle dance and the Cobla brass band are all kept alive here. It has produced no world-class classical masters, but it has a small yet active Andorran national youth orchestra and hosts international music festivals year-round (such as the Ordino Festival).

musicians.name: JONC d'Andorra
musicians.desc: Trained through the national youth orchestra system, it gives regular concerts and is the main vehicle for classical music in the valleys.

musicians.name: Marta Roure
musicians.desc: Andorra's most representative pop singer, who represented Andorra at the Eurovision Song Contest in 2004.

radios.name: Ràdio Nacional d'Andorra (RNA)
radios.note: Andorra's national radio, airing a wealth of Catalan-language music and local programming.

austria.name: Austria
austria.intro: Home of the 'City of Music', Vienna — a sanctuary and spiritual home of classical music.
history: Austria was once one of the most prominent powers on the European continent: the Habsburg dynasty made Vienna its heart, ruled the Holy Roman Empire for centuries, and founded the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Vienna thus became the political, artistic and cultural center of 18th–19th century Europe, radiating café culture, the waltz and the symphony across the continent.

After World War I the Austro-Hungarian Empire collapsed, and Austria shrank to today's Alpine republic; but its identity as a 'land of music and art' has never faded — the Vienna New Year's Concert, the Vienna Philharmonic and the Musikverein's Golden Hall remain shrines to music lovers worldwide.
music: The First Viennese School (Wiener Klassik) is the cornerstone of world music history: Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven and Schubert all lived and worked here, establishing the models of the symphony, string quartet and sonata. In the 19th century, the Strausses made the waltz Vienna's calling card, while Bruckner and Mahler pushed the symphony toward ever grander heights.

In the 20th century, Austria again became a center of modern music: Schoenberg, Berg and Webern founded the 'Second Viennese School', whose twelve-tone technique profoundly changed the course of music. The Vienna Philharmonic, the Vienna State Opera and the New Year's Concert every January 1 keep this city a place of pilgrimage for classical music to this day.

musicians.name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
musicians.desc: The summit of the Classical style, unsurpassed in symphony, opera, concerto and chamber music alike.

musicians.name: Franz Schubert
musicians.desc: The king of the art song (Lied), who left us 'The Trout', 'Winterreise' and the 'Unfinished' Symphony.

musicians.name: Gustav Mahler
musicians.desc: A titan of late Romanticism, famed for his vast and profound symphonies and symphonic song cycles.

musicians.name: Johann Strauss II
musicians.desc: The 'Waltz King', composer of 'The Blue Danube' and 'Voices of Spring', and the soul of the Vienna New Year's Concert.

musicians.name: Herbert von Karajan
musicians.desc: One of the most influential conductors of the 20th century, long at the helm of the Berlin Philharmonic and the maker of a vast legacy of classic recordings.

radios.name: Ö1
radios.note: The cultural and classical channel of the Austrian Broadcasting Corporation ORF, one of Europe's most authoritative public cultural stations.

belarus.name: Belarus
belarus.intro: A land of forests and lakes, the gentle soil of Slavic folk song.
history: Belarus lies on the East European Plain, the former land of Kievan Rus' and later of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, long situated at the meeting point of Eastern and Western powers. Annexed into the Soviet Union after World War II, it gained independence in 1991; its capital, Minsk, is known for its broad Stalinist avenues and tidy urban appearance.

The country is famed for its vast forests, wetlands and lakes, and is called part of 'Europe's lungs'. Slavic traditional culture survives here relatively intact, with folk embroidery, weaving and festive music still very much alive.
music: Belarusian folk music features polyphonic choral singing, ritual songs (such as those of the Kupala midsummer festival) and woodwinds with the dulcimer (cymbalom). In classical music, Belarus has produced no household names on the scale of Tchaikovsky, but it has a deep music-education system — the piano and violin schools of the Minsk Conservatory enjoy considerable prestige in Eastern Europe, and the State Philharmonic and the State Academic Folk Ensemble tour the world year-round.

musicians.name: Stanisław Moniuszko
musicians.desc: Born in the Minsk region of today's Belarus, he is hailed as the 'father of Polish national opera'; his opera 'Halka' has been profoundly influential.

musicians.name: State Academic Folk Ensemble
musicians.desc: Known for its grand choral singing and folk dance, it is the calling card that has carried Belarusian folk music to the world.

radios.name: Radio Belarus (Kultura)
radios.note: The cultural channel of Belarusian national radio, airing classical and folk music.

belgium.name: Belgium
belgium.intro: The heart of continental Europe, home of the jazz guitar and the saxophone, and a melting pot of electronic dance music and classical strings.
history: Belgium lies at the heart of Western Europe, historically ruled in turn by Burgundy, Spain, Austria and France before gaining independence in 1830 as one of the first industrialized countries on the continent. Today Brussels hosts the headquarters of both the EU and NATO and is called the 'capital of Europe'.

This trilingual kingdom (Dutch, French, German) is extraordinarily diverse; the Flemish and Walloon cultural spheres are at once separate and intertwined, and that very tension has bred an unusually open and creative artistic climate.
music: Belgium's contribution to music is often underestimated. Django Reinhardt, the god of jazz guitar, was of Roma heritage, yet it was here that he developed the entirely new genre of 'Gypsy Jazz'; the harmonica master Toots Thielemans and the father of the saxophone, Adolphe Sax, also came from Belgium. In the classical realm, Liège-born César Franck and the Franco-Belgian violin school (Vieuxtemps, Ysaÿe) shaped generations of string playing.

Contemporary Belgium is moreover a superpower of electronic music: Tomorrowland is the world's most prestigious electronic music festival, while Brussels-based techno and EDM producers have long dominated global dance charts. Classical and jazz, chanson and electronica coexist here in remarkable harmony.

musicians.name: César Franck
musicians.desc: A major composer of the French school; his Symphony in D minor and organ works have been profoundly influential.

musicians.name: Adolphe Sax
musicians.desc: The inventor of the saxophone, an instrument that later became the soulful voice of jazz.

musicians.name: Django Reinhardt
musicians.desc: The pioneer of Gypsy Jazz; despite injuring his left hand in a fire, he became one of the greatest guitarists in jazz history through astonishing technique.

musicians.name: Toots Thielemans
musicians.desc: A legend who brought the chromatic harmonica into the jazz mainstream, world-famous for 'Bluesette'.

musicians.name: Jacques Brel
musicians.desc: A giant of chanson, whose deep, powerful and theatrical singing captured the joys and sorrows of human life.

radios.name: Klara
radios.note: The classical and jazz channel of the Flemish public broadcaster VRT, of exceptionally high quality.

radios.name: Musiq3
radios.note: The classical channel of the French-language public broadcaster RTBF.

bosnia-and-herzegovina.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
bosnia-and-herzegovina.intro: The 'Jerusalem of Europe', a crossroads of Eastern and Western civilizations and the melancholic home of the sevdalinka love song.
history: Sarajevo is one of Europe's most symbolic cities: a bridge, a mosque, an Orthodox church and a Catholic church stand side by side, and for centuries Islamic, Orthodox, Catholic and Jewish cultures coexisted here — hence the name 'Jerusalem of Europe'. In 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated here, directly igniting World War I.

Bosnia and Herzegovina long lay under Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian rule; the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s inflicted deep wounds on this land, but today Sarajevo's old bridge and cobbled streets are coming back to life, and the memory of its multicultural coexistence remains vivid.
music: The most distinctive music of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the 'sevdalinka' — a melancholy urban love song of Ottoman origin, sung with long melodies, improvised ornamentation and accordion or oud accompaniment, telling of love, parting and nostalgia. Ensembles such as Mostar Sevdah Reunion have carried the tradition to the world.

The celebrated musician Goran Bregović was born in Sarajevo; fusing Balkan brass, Gypsy rhythms, rock and film scoring, he has become one of the most internationally recognizable names in Balkan music.

musicians.name: Goran Bregović
musicians.desc: Born in Sarajevo and the soul of the former band Bijelo Dugme, he is famed for film scores (such as 'Underground' and 'Time of the Gypsies') and is a global calling card of Balkan music.

musicians.name: Mostar Sevdah Reunion
musicians.desc: A sevdalinka ensemble from Mostar that has revived this ancient tradition of love song through authentic performance.

musicians.name: Dino Merlin
musicians.desc: One of Bosnia and Herzegovina's most successful pop musicians, having represented the country multiple times at the Eurovision Song Contest.

radios.name: BH Radio 1
radios.note: The main channel of the national broadcaster, airing a great deal of sevdalinka and traditional music.

bulgaria.name: Bulgaria
bulgaria.intro: Home of the 'Mystery Voices', with one of the world's most breathtaking traditions of women's choral singing.
history: Bulgaria lies in the eastern Balkans; its history reaches back to the 7th century BC, making it one of Europe's oldest countries. Long under Byzantine and Ottoman influence, it regained independence in the 19th century, preserving a deep Orthodox Christian culture and Thracian heritage.

The rose oil of the Rose Valley, yogurt (Lactobacillus bulgaricus) and the Thracian tombs are its cultural calling cards; and the irregular compound meters of its folk music (7/8, 9/8, 11/8 time) are a treasure unique in the history of world music.
music: What astonishes the world most about Bulgaria is its folk women's choral singing: the 'Bulgarian State Television Female Vocal Choir' stunned the West with the album 'Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares', whose piercing, slightly nasal dissonant harmonies and compound rhythms have captivated countless modern musicians, including Kate Bush.

In the classical realm, Bulgaria is a 'super-factory of operatic basses': world-class basses such as Boris Christoff and Nicolai Ghiaurov come from here; sopranos Raina Kabaivanska and Ghena Dimitrova are likewise celebrated worldwide.

musicians.name: Boris Christoff
musicians.desc: One of the greatest basses of the 20th century, famed for Russian operatic roles such as Boris Godunov.

musicians.name: Nicolai Ghiaurov
musicians.desc: A world-class bass, long active at La Scala, the Metropolitan and other leading opera houses.

musicians.name: Raina Kabaivanska
musicians.desc: A representative soprano interpreter of Italian opera, excelling in the works of Puccini and Verdi.

musicians.name: Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares
musicians.desc: Its heavenly dissonant harmonies and compound rhythms stunned the Western music world, becoming a legend of world music.

radios.name: BNR Hristo Botev
radios.note: The cultural channel of Bulgarian National Radio, giving equal weight to classical and folk music.

radios.name: Radio Bulgaria
radios.note: The external service, where one can hear authentic Bulgarian folk music.

croatia.name: Croatia
croatia.intro: The pearl of the Adriatic, birthplace of the klapa choir and the cello duo.
history: Croatia boasts a long, gorgeous Adriatic coastline; the old city of Dubrovnik, hailed as the 'Pearl of the Adriatic', also served as the filming location for King's Landing in 'Game of Thrones'. Historically part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire and Yugoslavia, it became independent in 1991.

Croatia belongs to both Central Europe and the Mediterranean; Zagreb's Central European character and Dalmatia's Mediterranean charm complement each other, and its multicultural heritage is exceptionally rich.
music: The 'klapa' of the Dalmatian region is an unaccompanied male polyphonic choir with flowing melodies and pure harmony; inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list around 2012, it has become Croatia's musical symbol. The 'Istrian scale' of the Istrian peninsula is likewise renowned for its distinctive non-tempered intervals.

In the classical realm, Croatia has produced two phenomenal pianists — Ivo Pogorelić and Maksim Mrvica — while the cello duo '2CELLOS' (Luka Šulić and Stjepan Hauser) brought the cello into popular culture.

musicians.name: Ivo Pogorelić
musicians.desc: Known for his idiosyncratic interpretations and astonishing technique, whose legendary status was ironically cemented by the controversy at the 1980 Chopin Competition.

musicians.name: Maksim Mrvica
musicians.desc: The 'crossover piano prince', a sensation across Asia with works such as 'Croatian Rhapsody' and 'Exodus'.

musicians.name: Luka Šulić & Stjepan Hauser
musicians.desc: The phenomenal duo that rockified the cello, bringing a classical instrument into the global pop spotlight.

radios.name: HRT HR3
radios.note: The third channel of Croatian Radio Television, devoted to classical, jazz and cultural programming.

cyprus.name: Cyprus
cyprus.intro: The island of Aphrodite in the eastern Mediterranean, a meeting point of Greek and Middle Eastern music.
history: Cyprus is the legendary birthplace of Aphrodite, goddess of love and beauty. Situated in the eastern Mediterranean, it has been a crossroads of Greek, Roman, Byzantine, Venetian and Ottoman civilizations for millennia. The island remains divided between its Greek and Turkish communities, and Nicosia is the world's last divided capital.
Rich historical remains — from the Neolithic site of Choirokoitia to Byzantine frescoed churches — make the island an open-air museum.
music: Cyprus's music features the Greek lyra (violi), the oud and 'tsiattista' (improvised sung duels), while also absorbing Middle Eastern and Anatolian colors. It has produced no world-class classical masters, but it has an active Cyprus Symphony Orchestra and hosts annual festivals such as the 'Paphos Aphrodite Festival' of opera and music.

musicians.name: Cyprus Symphony Orchestra
musicians.desc: The island's principal classical music institution, performing year-round in Nicosia and Limassol.

musicians.name: Michalis Hatzigiannis
musicians.desc: One of the most popular pop singers of the Greek-speaking world, hailing from Cyprus.

radios.name: RIK Triton / RIK Classic
radios.note: Channels of the Cyprus Broadcasting Corporation (RIK), balancing classical and local music.

czech-republic.name: Czech Republic
czech-republic.intro: Home of the 'City of a Hundred Spires', Prague — the land of Smetana and Dvořák, a heavyweight of European classical music.
history: The Czech Republic lies at the heart of Europe; Prague is hailed as the 'City of a Hundred Spires', its Old Town Square, Charles Bridge and Castle District preserving a complete panorama from the Middle Ages to the Baroque. Historically the core of the Kingdom of Bohemia, it underwent such 20th-century turning points as the Prague Spring.

Czechs care deeply about music and beer; per-capita beer consumption is perennially the highest in the world, and classical music permeates every corner of the city — Prague itself is one vast concert hall.
music: The Czech Republic is a true 'musical powerhouse'. Smetana's symphonic poem 'Má vlast' (including 'Vltava') is regarded as the symbol of the Czech national spirit; Dvořák's Symphony No. 9 'From the New World' and 'Slavonic Dances' are loved worldwide; Janáček and Martinů carried on this thread of nationalism intertwined with modern technique.

The annual 'Prague Spring' International Music Festival is one of Europe's most prestigious, opening on the anniversary of Smetana's death, May 12, with 'Má vlast', a tradition spanning more than half a century. The Czech violin school (Jan Kubelík, Josef Suk) has likewise been profoundly influential.

musicians.name: Bedřich Smetana
musicians.desc: The founder of the Czech national school and composer of 'Má vlast' and 'The Bartered Bride'.

musicians.name: Antonín Dvořák
musicians.desc: The Czech Republic's most celebrated composer, immortal through the 'New World' Symphony and 'Slavonic Dances'.

musicians.name: Leoš Janáček
musicians.desc: Creator of the distinctive 'speech melody' technique; his operas 'Jenůfa' and 'The Cunning Little Vixen' are strikingly modern.

musicians.name: Jan Kubelík
musicians.desc: An heir to the Paganini tradition, one of the greatest Czech violinists of the early 20th century.

radios.name: ČRo Vltava
radios.note: The cultural and classical channel of Czech Radio, one of Europe's finest public cultural stations.

radios.name: ČRo D-dur
radios.note: Czech Radio's dedicated classical channel.

denmark.name: Denmark
denmark.intro: A Nordic jazz stronghold, the fairytale kingdom of Hans Christian Andersen and Carl Nielsen.
history: Denmark is one of the oldest kingdoms in the Nordic region, home of the Viking descendants and of the fairytale master Hans Christian Andersen. Copenhagen is famed for the colorful houses of Nyhavn, the Little Mermaid statue and the 'hygge' way of life, and consistently ranks among the world's most livable cities.
Once a power of the North Sea and a partner in the Kalmar Union with Sweden and Norway, Denmark is known today for design, fine dining (Noma) and a high-welfare society.
music: In classical music, Carl Nielsen is Denmark's greatest composer, his six symphonies standing apart for their distinctive harmony and vigor. The Royal Danish Ballet is world-renowned for the choreographic tradition of Bournonville.

Even more remarkable is Danish jazz: Copenhagen is a major European jazz hub, and bass master Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen (NHØP) collaborated with numerous American jazz greats; the Copenhagen Jazz Festival is one of Europe's grandest jazz events.

musicians.name: Carl Nielsen
musicians.desc: Denmark's greatest composer; his six symphonies and the opera 'Maskarade' defined the heights of Nordic music.

musicians.name: Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen
musicians.desc: The benchmark of European jazz double bass, known for his lightning-fast fingering and singing lines.

musicians.name: Dieterich Buxtehude
musicians.desc: A Baroque organ master; the young Bach once walked hundreds of miles to hear him play.

radios.name: DR P2
radios.note: The classical and cultural channel of Danish Broadcasting.

radios.name: DR P8 Jazz
radios.note: Danish Broadcasting's jazz channel, full of Nordic jazz flavor.

estonia.name: Estonia
estonia.intro: The land of the 'Singing Revolution', birthplace of Arvo Pärt's bell-like tintinnabuli.
history: Estonia lies on the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea; Tallinn's Old Town is one of the best-preserved medieval cities in Northern Europe. Long under Danish, Swedish, German and Russian influence, it regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.

Estonians are known for the 'Singing Revolution': around 1988, hundreds of thousands gathered at Tallinn's Song Festival Grounds to voice their desire for independence through song, ultimately achieving a peaceful transformation. The Estonian Song Festival (Laulupidu), held every five years, remains one of the largest choral events in the world.
music: In classical music, Arvo Pärt is one of the most influential contemporary composers; his self-devised 'tintinnabuli' technique touches the heart with minimalist, sacred figures, and works such as 'Fratres' and 'Spiegel im Spiegel' are widely performed. The conductor Neeme Järvi and his family have likewise carried Estonia's conducting tradition to world renown.
Estonia's choral tradition runs deep; the sheer number and quality of its choirs are astonishing, inseparable from its history of the 'Singing Revolution'.

musicians.name: Arvo Pärt
musicians.desc: A leading figure of contemporary minimalism and sacred music, creator of the tintinnabuli technique and one of the most performed living composers in the world.

musicians.name: Neeme Järvi
musicians.desc: A prolific and authoritative conducting master; his sons Paavo and Kristjan Järvi are also renowned conductors.

musicians.name: Veljo Tormis
musicians.desc: Created a wealth of choral masterpieces drawn from the ancient folk songs of the Baltic Finns.

radios.name: Klassikaraadio
radios.note: The classical channel of Estonian Public Broadcasting (ERR).

finland.name: Finland
finland.intro: The 'Land of a Thousand Lakes', home of Sibelius's Nordic voice and a sanctuary of metal.
history: Finland is known as the 'Land of a Thousand Lakes'; its vast forests and lakes have shaped a calm, resilient national character. Long under Swedish and Russian rule, it gained independence in 1917, and its outnumbered resistance in the Winter War moved the world.
Finland is renowned for education, design (Marimekko, Iittala) and sauna culture, and is also a nation devoted to music — with one of the world's highest numbers of symphony orchestras per capita.
music: Jean Sibelius is Finland's national symbol; his 'Finlandia' became a patriotic rallying cry during the independence movement, while his seven symphonies and Violin Concerto are pinnacles of late Romanticism. Today Finland continues its strong classical tradition, with a conducting school (Salonen, Segerstam) and a steady stream of emerging composers.

Finland's other face is as the 'capital of heavy metal': bands such as Nightwish, HIM and Children of Bodom have made Finland the country with the most metal bands per capita in the world, and Helsinki even boasts the Tuska metal festival as a cultural landmark.

musicians.name: Jean Sibelius
musicians.desc: Finland's greatest composer; 'Finlandia', the Violin Concerto and seven symphonies are his enduring legacy.

musicians.name: Esa-Pekka Salonen
musicians.desc: A world-class conductor, long at the helm of the Los Angeles Philharmonic and now active with the San Francisco Symphony.

musicians.name: Nightwish
musicians.desc: A pioneer of 'symphonic metal', fusing operatic vocals with metal; global sales exceed ten million.

radios.name: Yle Klassinen
radios.note: The classical channel of the Finnish Broadcasting Company YLE.

radios.name: Yle Radio 1
radios.note: YLE's cultural channel, airing a wealth of classical and arts programming.

france.name: France
france.intro: A land of art and cuisine, the elegant home of Impressionist music, chanson and jazz.
history: France is one of the centers of European civilization; Paris is called the 'City of Light'. From the Versailles of Louis XIV to the French Revolution, from the Enlightenment to Impressionist painting, France has profoundly shaped the politics, art and thought of the modern world.

French culture is famed for refinement and taste: cuisine, fashion, literature and music nourish one another here, and for centuries the cafés, salons and opera houses of Paris have been the spiritual home of artists.
music: French music has its own distinctive elegance and color. From Berlioz's 'Symphonie fantastique', Saint-Saëns's 'Carnival of the Animals' and Bizet's 'Carmen', to the Impressionism pioneered by Debussy and Ravel, the French shaped the entire 20th century through delicate orchestral color and harmonic innovation. Satie, Poulenc, Messiaen and Boulez carried on this thread of perpetual renewal.

Chanson is the soulful voice of the French: the songs of Édith Piaf ('La Vie en rose'), Charles Aznavour and Georges Brassens have carried the emotions of generations. And stations such as FIP and TSF Jazz have turned an aesthetic of 'elegant, eclectic and niche' programming into a global calling card.

musicians.name: Claude Debussy
musicians.desc: The pioneer of Impressionist music; 'Clair de Lune' and 'Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune' revolutionized the language of harmony with hazy color.

musicians.name: Maurice Ravel
musicians.desc: A master of orchestration; 'Boléro' and 'Daphnis et Chloé' display matchless orchestral color.

musicians.name: Édith Piaf
musicians.desc: The 'Little Sparrow', the embodiment of French chanson; 'La Vie en rose' and 'Hymne à l'amour' are sung to this day.

musicians.name: Hector Berlioz
musicians.desc: A pioneer of Romantic program music; 'Symphonie fantastique' opened a new orchestral language.

musicians.name: Erik Satie
musicians.desc: Known for spare, whimsical piano miniatures such as the 'Gymnopédies', which influenced later minimalism.

radios.name: France Musique
radios.note: France's most authoritative classical music station, of exceptionally high programming quality.

radios.name: FIP
radios.note: A 'hip' station famed for its impeccable taste — ad-free, genre-crossing selection, a shrine for music lovers worldwide.

radios.name: Radio Classique
radios.note: A well-known French classical station.

radios.name: TSF Jazz
radios.note: One of France's purest jazz stations.

germany.name: Germany
germany.intro: The center of gravity of classical music, the great homeland of Bach, Beethoven and Brahms.
history: Germany is unquestionably the center of gravity of European classical music. From the Baroque Bach and Handel, through the Beethoven of the First Viennese School, to the Romantics Schumann, Mendelssohn, Brahms and Wagner, Germany has written much of the history of Western art music.

Beyond music, Germany is a powerhouse of philosophy, literature (Goethe, Schiller) and industrial manufacturing; Berlin, Munich, Hamburg, Dresden and Leipzig each possess world-class orchestras and opera houses.
music: Germany's musical heritage runs extraordinarily deep: the Berlin Philharmonic is widely regarded as the world's finest orchestra, while the Leipzig Gewandhaus and Dresden Staatskapelle count centuries of history; Bach's own St. Thomas Boys Choir in Leipzig still sings his cantatas to this day.

Since the 20th century, Germany has been both a stronghold of modern music (Hindemith, Stockhausen) and the cradle of electronic music (Kraftwerk); Berlin has moreover become a global center of techno and club culture.

musicians.name: Johann Sebastian Bach
musicians.desc: The supreme master of Baroque music, revered as the 'father of music'; his fugues and cantatas reached the summit of polyphony.

musicians.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
musicians.desc: A giant spanning the Classical and Romantic eras; his nine symphonies and the 'Moonlight' and 'Appassionata' sonatas are monuments of the human spirit.

musicians.name: Johannes Brahms
musicians.desc: One of the 'Three Bs'; his four symphonies and 'A German Requiem' combine classical structure with Romantic depth.

musicians.name: Richard Wagner
musicians.desc: A reformer of opera who, through his concept of the 'music drama', created monumental works such as 'Der Ring des Nibelungen'.

musicians.name: Robert Schumann
musicians.desc: A double giant of Romantic music and music criticism, with towering achievements in piano works and art song.

radios.name: BR-Klassik
radios.note: The classical channel of Bavarian Broadcasting, a benchmark among European classical stations.

radios.name: Deutschlandfunk Kultur
radios.note: Germany's national cultural station, giving equal weight to music, drama and ideas.

radios.name: WDR 3
radios.note: The cultural channel of West German Broadcasting.

radios.name: hr2-kultur
radios.note: The cultural channel of Hessian Broadcasting.

greece.name: Greece
greece.intro: The cradle of Western civilization, home of the rebetiko lament and the dance of Zorba.
history: Greece is the cradle of Western civilization: democracy, philosophy, drama and the Olympic Games were all born here, and the Acropolis and Parthenon in Athens bear witness to millennia of splendor. It is also the heir of the Orthodox world and Byzantine civilization, and modern Greece gained independence from the Ottoman Empire in the 19th century.
The thousands of Aegean islands, the blue-and-white Santorini and ancient mythological traditions make Greece one of the places most laden with the memory of human civilization.
music: Greece's most distinctive music is 'rebetiko' — an urban lament born in the port underworld of the early 20th century, accompanied by the bouzouki and telling of exile, poverty and the bitterness of love; it was inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2017.

In the classical realm, Greece gave the world the 'opera goddess' Maria Callas, the composers Mikis Theodorakis ('Zorba the Greek') and Manos Hatzidakis; while electronic music pioneer Vangelis won global fame with his scores for 'Chariots of Fire' and 'Blade Runner'.

musicians.name: Maria Callas
musicians.desc: The 'opera goddess' and the most legendary singer of the 20th century, who reshaped the standards of bel canto performance.

musicians.name: Mikis Theodorakis
musicians.desc: Famed for the 'Zorba's Dance' from 'Zorba the Greek', and a cultural symbol of resistance to dictatorship.

musicians.name: Vangelis
musicians.desc: A master of electronic music and film scoring; his scores for 'Chariots of Fire' and 'Blade Runner' are deeply affecting.

musicians.name: Dimitris Mitropoulos
musicians.desc: The head of the New York Philharmonic in the mid-20th century, known for his astonishing ability to conduct from memory.

radios.name: ERT Third Programme
radios.note: The cultural channel of Hellenic Broadcasting, featuring classical music and arts programming.

radios.name: Kosmos 93.6
radios.note: ERT's world music channel, rich in rebetiko and Mediterranean sounds.

hungary.name: Hungary
hungary.intro: The homeland of Liszt, Bartók and Kodály, a musical powerhouse on the Danube.
history: Hungary is the Magyar nation of central Europe; Budapest is famed for the Parliament Building on the Danube, the Chain Bridge and its thermal baths. It once formed the Austro-Hungarian Empire with Austria, and endured two world wars and upheaval in the 20th century, yet its musical tradition has remained unbroken.
Hungarian stands alone within the Indo-European family (it belongs to the Uralic family), and this 'linguistic island' quality is mirrored in its distinctive and powerful folk music.
music: Hungary's contribution to world music is astonishing. Liszt is the giant of Romantic piano, his 'Hungarian Rhapsodies' bringing folk melody into the concert hall; Bartók and Kodály traveled deep into the countryside to collect folk music, laying the foundations of modern ethnomusicology.

In conducting, Hungary is a veritable 'cradle of conductors': masters such as Solti, Szell, Doráti and Ormándy all come from here. Budapest's Liszt Academy of Music remains one of Europe's most important conservatories.

musicians.name: Franz Liszt
musicians.desc: The king of Romantic piano; he created the 'symphonic poem' and his virtuosity and harmonic innovations were profoundly influential.

musicians.name: Béla Bartók
musicians.desc: One of the most important composers of the 20th century, fusing folk music with modern technique.

musicians.name: Zoltán Kodály
musicians.desc: Founder of the 'Kodály method', which has profoundly influenced music education worldwide.

musicians.name: Georg Solti
musicians.desc: Once head of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra; his recording of the 'Ring' is hailed as one of the greatest opera recordings in history.

radios.name: Bartók Rádió (MR3)
radios.note: The classical channel of Hungarian Radio, named after Bartók.

radios.name: Kossuth Rádió (MR1)
radios.note: The main channel of Hungarian Radio, balancing folk music and news.

iceland.name: Iceland
iceland.intro: A land of auroras and glaciers, the poetic home of Björk, Sigur Rós and ambient music.
history: Iceland is an island of volcanoes and glaciers in the North Atlantic; Reykjavík is the world's northernmost capital. Vikings settled here in the 9th century and founded one of the world's oldest parliaments (the Althing).
Iceland's geothermal hot springs, auroras and lava landscapes form a surreal natural world, and this ethereal, primal environment has profoundly shaped its musical temperament.
music: Iceland's musical output and quality are wildly disproportionate to its population of 380,000. Björk has become a global icon through her wildly imaginative experimental pop; the post-rock band Sigur Rós sings in an invented 'Hopelandic' tongue, conjuring otherworldly soundscapes; and composers Jóhann Jóhannsson (score for 'The Theory of Everything') and Ólafur Arnalds have fused classical, electronic and minimalism into a highly distinctive 'Icelandic sound'.
In the classical realm, the Iceland Symphony Orchestra and the Harpa concert hall have made Reykjavík an important Nordic music hub.

musicians.name: Björk
musicians.desc: Iceland's most internationally influential musician, known for pioneering electronic pop and visual art.

musicians.name: Sigur Rós
musicians.desc: Known for its ethereal, far-reaching post-rock and singing in a self-invented language, a symbol of Iceland's sound.

musicians.name: Jóhann Jóhannsson
musicians.desc: A master of film scoring; 'The Theory of Everything' won a Golden Globe, and his 'Arrival' score is richly atmospheric.

musicians.name: Ólafur Arnalds
musicians.desc: A representative of the fusion of classical, electronic and ambient music, whose works are cool and healing.

radios.name: Rás 1
radios.note: The cultural channel of Icelandic National Broadcasting, airing classical and Icelandic music.

radios.name: Rás 2
radios.note: The music channel of Icelandic National Broadcasting.

ireland.name: Ireland
ireland.intro: The heart of Celtic music — an emerald isle of bagpipes, fiddle and Enya.
history: Ireland is known as the 'Emerald Isle', where Celtic culture has endured for millennia. Long under British rule, it gained independence in 1922, but its traditions of music, literature and language have never been broken.
Dublin is the home of literary giants such as Joyce, Yeats and Beckett, and the site of the world's largest St. Patrick's Day celebrations; its Celtic music and dance culture are renowned worldwide.
music: Irish traditional music is built on the uilleann pipes, fiddle, tin whistle and bodhrán, with lively jigs and reels as its soul; 'Riverdance' carried Irish step dancing to the world.
In the classical realm, John Field invented the nocturne; in pop, Enya, U2, Sinéad O'Connor and Van Morrison have made Ireland a vital source of English-language popular music.

musicians.name: John Field
musicians.desc: The creator of the nocturne, who profoundly influenced the later Chopin.

musicians.name: Enya
musicians.desc: A goddess of New Age music, known for her layered vocals and ethereal arrangements.

musicians.name: U2
musicians.desc: Ireland's greatest rock band, with global sales of over 150 million.

musicians.name: The Chieftains
musicians.desc: The banner that carried Irish traditional music to the world, winner of six Grammy Awards.

radios.name: RTÉ Lyric FM
radios.note: The classical and arts channel of Irish broadcasting, of high quality.

radios.name: RTÉ Radio 1
radios.note: The main channel of Irish broadcasting, frequently featuring traditional music programs.

italy.name: Italy
italy.intro: The birthplace of opera, the eternal land of Verdi, Puccini and the Renaissance.
history: Italy is one of the most important sources of Western civilization: the Roman Empire, the Renaissance, opera and cuisine all went out into the world from here. Rome, Florence, Venice and Milan are each monuments of human art.
The Italian love of beauty and life runs to the marrow; from arias at La Scala to espresso at a street café, art is everywhere.
music: Italy is the home of opera: Monteverdi established the form, Rossini, Donizetti and Bellini founded the bel canto tradition, and Verdi and Puccini carried opera to the heights of drama and emotion — 'La traviata', 'Rigoletto', 'Turandot' and 'Madama Butterfly' are performed to this day.

Beyond opera, Vivaldi's 'Four Seasons', Paganini's violin virtuosity and Scarlatti's keyboard sonatas all come from Italy; in film scoring, the melodies of Morricone and Rota have become classics of cinema history.

musicians.name: Giuseppe Verdi
musicians.desc: The summit of Italian opera, composer of 'La traviata', 'Rigoletto' and 'Aida'.

musicians.name: Giacomo Puccini
musicians.desc: Moved the world with lyrical operas such as 'Turandot', 'Madama Butterfly' and 'La bohème'.

musicians.name: Antonio Vivaldi
musicians.desc: The 'Red Priest', a Baroque concerto master; 'The Four Seasons' is among the most famous classical works in history.

musicians.name: Niccolò Paganini
musicians.desc: A legend of violin technique; his '24 Caprices' remain a touchstone for players today.

musicians.name: Ennio Morricone
musicians.desc: A master of Spaghetti Western scores; the whistled theme of 'The Good, the Bad and the Ugly' is known to all.

radios.name: Rai Radio 3 Classica
radios.note: The classical channel of Italian national radio (RAI).

radios.name: Radio Classica
radios.note: A well-known Italian classical station.

radios.name: Rai Radio 3
radios.note: The cultural channel of Italian national radio.

latvia.name: Latvia
latvia.intro: A Baltic land of folk song, home of the daina tradition and conducting masters.
history: Latvia lies on the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea; Riga's Old Town is a World Heritage site, with especially exquisite Art Nouveau architecture. Historically influenced in turn by Germany, Sweden and Russia, it regained independence in 1991.
Latvians treasure their 'daina' — a tradition of over a million short folk songs, hailed as one of the world's greatest treasuries of folk song and inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
music: Latvia's choral and folk-song traditions run exceptionally deep, and its quinquennial National Song and Dance Festival is the grandest cultural event in the Baltics. In the classical realm, Latvia has produced a number of world-class musicians: conductor Mariss Jansons, violinist Gidon Kremer and cellist Mischa Maisky all hail from here.

musicians.name: Mariss Jansons
musicians.desc: One of the most respected conducting masters of the late 20th century, long at the helm of the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra and the Bavarian Radio Symphony Orchestra.

musicians.name: Gidon Kremer
musicians.desc: Known for profound interpretations and advocacy of modern music; founder of the Kremerata Baltica chamber orchestra.

musicians.name: Mischa Maisky
musicians.desc: A Latvian-born cello master and student of Rostropovich, whose playing is passionate and songful.

radios.name: Latvijas Radio 3 - Klasika
radios.note: The classical channel of Latvian Radio.

lithuania.name: Lithuania
lithuania.intro: The birthplace of Heifetz, a land of Čiurlionis and Baltic folk song.
history: Lithuania was once one of the most powerful states of medieval Europe, its territory stretching at times from the Baltic to the Black Sea. Vilnius Old Town is one of Europe's largest Baroque old towns; in 1991 Lithuania was the first to break away from the Soviet Union, setting the Baltic states on the road to freedom.

Lithuanian is one of the oldest living languages and closest to Proto-Indo-European, an antiquity reflected in its distinctive folk-song tradition (such as the Sutartinės polyphonic songs, inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list).
music: In classical music, M. K. Čiurlionis was both composer and painter, his music and painting interpenetrating and making him a spiritual symbol of Lithuania. Jascha Heifetz, one of the greatest violinists of the 20th century, was also born in Vilnius.
Contemporary Lithuania's conducting tradition is equally dazzling, with a new generation such as Mirga Gražinytė-Tyla rising on the international stage.

musicians.name: M. K. Čiurlionis
musicians.desc: A national treasure of Lithuania, whose symphonic poems and paintings are steeped in mysticism.

musicians.name: Jascha Heifetz
musicians.desc: Born in Vilnius and widely regarded as the greatest violinist of the 20th century, with peerless technique.

musicians.name: Mirga Gražinytė-Tyla
musicians.desc: A rising conducting star, formerly music director of the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra.

radios.name: LRT Klasika
radios.note: The classical and cultural channel of Lithuanian National Radio and Television.

liechtenstein.name: Liechtenstein
liechtenstein.intro: A doubly landlocked Alpine state, echoing with brass bands and pastoral music.
history: Liechtenstein is one of Europe's smallest countries, wedged between Switzerland and Austria, and one of the world's rare 'doubly landlocked' states (landlocked itself, with landlocked neighbors on all sides). It is known for low taxes, precision industry and its princely castle; Vaduz Castle sits high on the mountainside, overlooking the Rhine Valley.
In this principality of just over 39,000 people, the head of state still lives in the castle, and life is prosperous and tranquil, suffused with Alpine pastoral charm.
music: Liechtenstein has produced no world-class classical masters, but it has a lively tradition of brass bands (Blasmusik) and church choirs; village festivals and religious ceremonies form the backbone of its musical life. Closely tied to the music scenes of Switzerland and Austria, Vaduz also regularly hosts small music festivals.

musicians.name: Liechtenstein Brass Bands
musicians.desc: Traditional Alpine brass bands that are the musical mainstay of Liechtenstein's festivals and religious occasions.

radios.name: Radio Liechtenstein
radios.note: The national radio station, airing local news and music programs.

luxembourg.name: Luxembourg
luxembourg.intro: Europe's wealthiest tiny grand duchy, once a legendary name in European pop broadcasting.
history: Luxembourg is one of Europe's richest countries, situated between Germany, France and Belgium and historically a buffer between the great powers. Its capital's old town and fortifications are a World Heritage site, and it is now home to major EU institutions.
With just over 600,000 inhabitants, this small country has long ranked among the world's highest in GDP per capita, with finance and steel once its mainstays.
music: Luxembourg has produced no world-class classical masters, but it left a vivid mark on broadcasting history: from after World War II to the 1990s, 'Radio Luxembourg' was one of Europe's most influential commercial pop stations, broadcasting pop music in English to Britain and all of Europe and profoundly shaping the spread of rock and pop.
Today the Orchestre Philharmonique du Luxembourg performs in its new Philharmonie hall and ranks among the finest of Europe's mid-generation orchestras.

musicians.name: Orchestre Philharmonique du Luxembourg
musicians.desc: Luxembourg's principal classical institution, frequently collaborating with internationally renowned soloists and conductors.

radios.name: Radio 100,7
radios.note: Luxembourg's public broadcaster, airing classical and local cultural programming.

malta.name: Malta
malta.intro: The knights' island at the heart of the Mediterranean, home of tenor Joseph Calleja.
history: Malta sits at the center of the Mediterranean; historically an outpost of the Phoenicians, Romans, Arabs and the Knights of St. John, its capital Valletta was built by the Knights in the 16th century and is inscribed in its entirety as a World Heritage site.
As a crossroads, Malta's language and culture fuse European and North African elements; Maltese is Europe's only Semitic-family language.
music: Malta has a long operatic tradition, and the Manoel Theatre (1731) is one of Europe's oldest theaters still in use. Its most dazzling contemporary star is the tenor Joseph Calleja, hailed for his 'golden voice' and active at the world's leading opera houses.

musicians.name: Joseph Calleja
musicians.desc: Malta's national-treasure tenor, known for his lustrous, metallic voice, and a regular at the Metropolitan and Covent Garden.

radios.name: PBS Radju Malta
radios.note: Malta's public broadcaster, balancing classical and local music.

moldova.name: Moldova
moldova.intro: A land of vineyards and folk song, the eastern wing of the Romanian cultural sphere.
history: Moldova lies between Romania and Ukraine; historically part of the Principality of Moldavia, it later long belonged to Russia and the Soviet Union. It is famed for its fertile black soil, vineyards and underground wine cellars.
This small Eastern European country shares language and ethnicity with Romania, with intertwined languages, folk songs and customs.
music: Moldovan music features the Romanian 'doina' lyrical folk song, the hora circle dance and the cimbalom. In the classical realm, soprano Maria Bieșu is Moldova's most celebrated singer, long active on the opera stages of Chișinău and Moscow.

musicians.name: Maria Bieșu
musicians.desc: Moldova's most famous operatic soprano; her name graces the national opera house in Chișinău.

radios.name: Radio Moldova
radios.note: Moldova's national radio, airing a great deal of folk music.

monaco.name: Monaco
monaco.intro: A luxurious principality on the Mediterranean coast, a glittering temple of Monte-Carlo opera and jazz.
history: Monaco is the world's second-smallest country, yet it is globally famous for the Monte-Carlo Casino, the Monaco Grand Prix of Formula One and its royal family (the House of Grimaldi). Facing the Mediterranean and backed by the Alps, it is synonymous with luxury and elegance.
Tiny as it is, this city-state has an extraordinarily high cultural density, and Princess Grace (Grace Kelly) bound it forever to Hollywood.
music: Monaco's Opéra de Monte-Carlo has a long history and, together with the Monte-Carlo Philharmonic Orchestra, forms the Mediterranean coast's most dazzling classical stage; the Monte-Carlo Jazz Festival is one of Europe's celebrated jazz events.

musicians.name: Orchestre Philharmonique de Monte-Carlo
musicians.desc: The princely orchestra of Monaco, collaborating year-round with top soloists and enjoying a highly prestigious season.

radios.name: Riviera Radio
radios.note: An English-language station covering Monaco and the Côte d'Azur, airing a wealth of jazz and easy listening.

montenegro.name: Montenegro
montenegro.intro: A land of mountains on the Adriatic coast, home of the gusle epic chant.
history: Montenegro (Crna Gora, meaning 'Black Mountain') is famed for its rugged mountains and the Adriatic fjord of the Bay of Kotor, whose old town is a World Heritage site. Long independent, it separated from the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro in 2006.
Montenegro is one of the smallest of the former Yugoslav states, yet it possesses a rich history and magnificent nature.
music: Montenegro's most distinctive musical tradition is the 'gusle' — heroic epics sung to a single-stringed bowed instrument, telling of ancient battles and legends, inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list. The KotorArt festival is one of Southeast Europe's important classical music events.

musicians.name: KotorArt Festival
musicians.desc: An international arts festival held in the old town of Kotor, spanning classical music, theater and visual arts.

radios.name: Radio Crne Gore
radios.note: Montenegro's national radio, airing folk music and cultural programming.

netherlands.name: Netherlands
netherlands.intro: A land of canals and windmills, home of the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra and a shrine of electronic dance music.
history: The Netherlands was the 'carrier of the seas', the maritime overlord of the 17th-century Golden Age and the home of painting masters such as Rembrandt and Vermeer. Amsterdam's canal ring is a World Heritage site, and windmills, tulips and bicycles form its classic imagery.
The Dutch are known for openness, pragmatism and tolerance, qualities that permeate their diverse and avant-garde music culture.
music: In classical music, the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra is widely regarded as one of the world's finest, and its hall's acoustics are legendary. The Netherlands also gave us the Baroque organ master Sweelinck and several conducting giants (Haitink among them).

The Netherlands is moreover a global center of electronic music: top DJs such as Tiësto, Armin van Buuren, Hardwell and Martin Garrix all come from here, and the Amsterdam Dance Event (ADE) is an annual highlight of the electronic music world. In jazz, Sublime radio and the North Sea Jazz Festival are likewise world-renowned.

musicians.name: Jan Pieterszoon Sweelinck
musicians.desc: A Baroque organ master, hailed as the 'father of the North German organ school'.

musicians.name: Bernard Haitink
musicians.desc: One of the greatest conductors of the 20th century, long at the helm of the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra.

musicians.name: Tiësto
musicians.desc: One of the most influential DJs in electronic dance music, repeatedly ranked No. 1 on the DJ Mag Top 100.

musicians.name: André Rieu
musicians.desc: A global sensation through the waltz tours of his 'Johann Strauss Orchestra', bringing classical music to the masses.

radios.name: NPO Radio 4
radios.note: The classical channel of Dutch public broadcasting.

radios.name: Sublime
radios.note: The Netherlands' most famous jazz and soul station.

north-macedonia.name: North Macedonia
north-macedonia.intro: A Balkan crossroads, a land of the rhythms of the tapan drum and the zurla.
history: North Macedonia lies in the heart of the Balkans; historically a frontier of the Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman empires, the stark contrast between Skopje's old and new quarters is a microcosm of its turbulent history. In 2019 it was renamed North Macedonia, ending its years-long name dispute with Greece.
Lake Ohrid is one of Europe's oldest and deepest lakes, and the icons and churches on its shores bear witness to a millennium of Orthodox tradition.
music: North Macedonian music is most distinctive in its wedding, funeral and festival music of the 'tapan' (large drum) and 'zurla' (double-reed woodwind), its irregular Balkan compound rhythms captivating. Pop singer Toše Proeski was one of the Balkans' most beloved idols.

musicians.name: Toše Proeski
musicians.desc: A household-name pop idol across the Balkans, hailed as the 'Nightingale of the Balkans', who died young.

radios.name: MRT Radio Skopje
radios.note: North Macedonia's national radio, airing folk music.

norway.name: Norway
norway.intro: A land of fjords, home of Grieg's Nordic romanticism and the cool poetry of ECM jazz.
history: Norway is famed for its magnificent fjords, auroras and midnight sun, from which the Vikings once sailed. Long in union with Denmark and Sweden, it gained independence in 1905 and is now one of the world's wealthiest and happiest countries.
Norwegians live close to nature, and the polar night of winter and midnight sun of summer have shaped the distinctive chill and vastness of its music.
music: In classical music, Edvard Grieg is Norway's greatest composer; his 'Peer Gynt' suites and Piano Concerto in A minor are masterpieces of Nordic Romanticism. The violinist Ole Bull was a 19th-century virtuoso.

Norwegian jazz, flying the banner of the ECM label, is led by figures such as Jan Garbarek and Terje Rypdal, who pioneered the cool, ethereal 'Nordic jazz' aesthetic; moreover, a-ha's 'Take On Me' and Norwegian black metal have each influenced the world in their own spheres.

musicians.name: Edvard Grieg
musicians.desc: Norway's greatest composer; the 'Morning Mood' of his 'Peer Gynt' suites is universally beloved.

musicians.name: Jan Garbarek
musicians.desc: A standard-bearer of the ECM label, whose ethereal, far-reaching saxophone defined the 'Nordic jazz' sound.

musicians.name: Ole Bull
musicians.desc: A 19th-century violin prodigy, hailed as the 'Paganini of the North'.

radios.name: NRK Klassisk
radios.note: The classical channel of Norwegian Broadcasting.

radios.name: NRK Jazz
radios.note: The jazz channel of Norwegian Broadcasting.

poland.name: Poland
poland.intro: The homeland of Chopin, a great home of Romantic piano and modern music.
history: Poland lies in Central Europe; repeatedly partitioned by the great powers in history, it has nonetheless maintained a tenacious national identity. Warsaw's Old Town was rebuilt almost perfectly after World War II and is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
From Copernicus to Marie Curie, from Chopin to Pope John Paul II, Poland has given the world countless remarkable figures.
music: The heart of Polish music is unquestionably Frédéric Chopin — the 'poet of the piano' who wove Polish mazurkas and polonaises into the keyboard and became the embodiment of Romantic piano. The International Chopin Piano Competition in Warsaw remains one of the most important events in the piano world.
In the 20th century, Poland also nurtured modern-music giants such as Penderecki, Lutosławski and Górecki, as well as a generation of piano masters including Rubinstein and Zimerman.

musicians.name: Frédéric Chopin
musicians.desc: The 'poet of the piano', the perfect embodiment of the nocturne, mazurka, polonaise and étude.

musicians.name: Krzysztof Penderecki
musicians.desc: A giant of 20th-century modern music; his 'Threnody to the Victims of Hiroshima' stunned the world.

musicians.name: Arthur Rubinstein
musicians.desc: One of the greatest pianists of the 20th century and an authoritative interpreter of Chopin.

musicians.name: Henryk Wieniawski
musicians.desc: A Romantic violin virtuoso whose concertos and caprices are still performed today.

radios.name: Dwójka (PR2)
radios.note: The second channel of Polish Radio, an authoritative station for classical music and culture.

radios.name: Radio Chopin
radios.note: A classical station named after Chopin.

portugal.name: Portugal
portugal.intro: The melancholy land of fado, with the musical afterglow of the Age of Discovery.
history: Portugal was a pioneer of the Age of Discovery; Vasco da Gama and Magellan set out from here to explore the world, and Lisbon's Belém Tower and Jerónimos Monastery bear witness to that golden age. It once built an empire spanning several continents and retains deep cultural ties with Brazil and the Portuguese-speaking countries of Africa.
Lisbon's cobbled alleys and fado houses, and Porto's port wine cellars, form this Iberian country's distinctive melancholy and romance.
music: 'Fado' is the soulful voice of Portugal — an urban lament steeped in 'Saudade' (longing/nostalgia), usually accompanied by the Portuguese guitar (guitarra portuguesa), which Amália Rodrigues turned into a national treasure.
In the classical realm, Portugal produced the Baroque keyboard composer Carlos Seixas and one of the most respected contemporary pianists, Maria João Pires; its jazz tradition is also deep-rooted.

musicians.name: Amália Rodrigues
musicians.desc: The 'Queen of Fado', who carried fado from Lisbon's taverns to the world; fado was inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2011.

musicians.name: Maria João Pires
musicians.desc: One of the finest pianists of our time, renowned for her interpretations of Mozart and Chopin.

musicians.name: Carlos Seixas
musicians.desc: A representative of Portuguese Baroque keyboard music, contemporary with Scarlatti yet distinctive in style.

radios.name: Antena 2
radios.note: The classical and cultural channel of Portuguese broadcasting.

radios.name: Rádio Amália
radios.note: A station devoted entirely to fado music.

romania.name: Romania
romania.intro: The land of Enescu and the doina, the far-reaching home of the pan flute.
history: Romania lies in Southeastern Europe, the Carpathian Mountains running through it; the castles of Transylvania (such as Bran Castle) and their legends lend it an air of romance. As descendants of the Latins, it has kept its Romance heritage amid a Slavic and Balkan world.
From the 'Little Paris' charm of Bucharest to the wooden churches of Maramureș, Romania's cultural landscape is extraordinarily diverse.
music: Romania's most nationally distinctive music is the 'doina' — a free-rhythm improvised lyric — and the pan-flute master Gheorghe Zamfir carried it across the world.

In the classical realm, George Enescu is Romania's greatest composer and violinist, his 'Romanian Rhapsodies' known to all; pianist Dinu Lipatti and soprano Angela Gheorghiu are likewise world-class names.

musicians.name: George Enescu
musicians.desc: Romania's greatest musician; the Enescu Festival in Bucharest is named after him.

musicians.name: Dinu Lipatti
musicians.desc: Hailed as a 'poet of the piano', leaving immortal recordings of Chopin and Bach despite his early death.

musicians.name: Angela Gheorghiu
musicians.desc: One of the finest operatic sopranos of our time, known for Puccini and Verdi.

musicians.name: Gheorghe Zamfir
musicians.desc: The 'King of the Pan Flute', who carried Romania's pan flute to the world stage.

radios.name: Radio România Muzical
radios.note: The classical music channel of Romanian Radio.

radios.name: Radio România Cultural
radios.note: The cultural channel of Romanian Radio.

russia.name: Russia
russia.intro: The homeland of Tchaikovsky and Rachmaninoff, the majestic home of Slavic Romanticism.
history: Russia spans Europe and Asia and is the largest country in the world by area. From Tsarist Russia through the Soviet Union to today's federation, it has always been a major force shaping world affairs. The Kremlin in Moscow and the Winter Palace in St. Petersburg bear witness to centuries of momentous history.
Russian culture is known for its depth, weight and vastness; literature (Tolstoy, Dostoevsky), ballet and music together form its immortal spiritual legacy.
music: Russian classical music holds immense weight in the world: Glinka founded the national school, Tchaikovsky's ballets ('Swan Lake', 'The Nutcracker') and symphonies conquered the globe, and then came Rachmaninoff's piano concertos, Mussorgsky's 'Pictures at an Exhibition', Rimsky-Korsakov's orchestral color, the 20th-century masterpieces of Prokofiev and Shostakovich, and Stravinsky's 'The Rite of Spring' — every one of these names is a monument.
Russia's piano and conducting schools, and the ballet traditions of the Mariinsky Theatre and the Bolshoi, make it equally peerless in the performing arts.

musicians.name: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
musicians.desc: One of Romanticism's greatest melodists; 'Swan Lake' and the 'Pathétique' Symphony are his enduring legacy.

musicians.name: Sergei Rachmaninoff
musicians.desc: A late-Romantic giant; his Second and Third Piano Concertos are deeply moving.

musicians.name: Dmitri Shostakovich
musicians.desc: One of the most important symphonists of the 20th century, whose works burst with power amid repression.

musicians.name: Igor Stravinsky
musicians.desc: The premiere of 'The Rite of Spring' caused a sensation; he is one of the most influential innovators in modern music.

musicians.name: Modest Mussorgsky
musicians.desc: A member of 'The Five'; 'Pictures at an Exhibition' and 'Boris Godunov' are rugged and profound.

radios.note: Russia's national classical music station, the classical channel of the Russian broadcasting group.

radios.note: The cultural channel of Russian national radio.

san-marino.name: San Marino
san-marino.intro: The world's oldest republic, a city of music festivals among hilltop castles.
history: Surrounded by Italy, San Marino claims to be the world's oldest republic, founded in AD 301. It sits atop Mount Titano, its three castles overlooking the Apennine mountains, and its entire historic center is a World Heritage site.
This tiny state of just over 30,000 people is known for freedom, independence and ancient political traditions.
music: Small as it is, San Marino has its own San Marino International Music Festival, drawing young musicians from around the world; its military band and brass tradition are also well known.

musicians.name: San Marino International Music Festival
musicians.desc: An international music festival held in the castle-ringed republic, spanning classical and chamber music.

radios.name: Radio San Marino
radios.note: The national radio of San Marino, airing local and Italian-language programming.

serbia.name: Serbia
serbia.intro: The feverish home of the Guča Trumpet Festival and the kolo dance, the epicenter of Balkan rhythm.
history: Serbia lies at the core of the Balkans; Belgrade sits at the confluence of the Sava and Danube rivers, historically the 'gateway to the Balkans' contested by Eastern and Western powers. It was the core of Yugoslavia and became independent in 2006.
Belgrade is famed for its nightlife and warmth; the bars and clubs along the Sava make it one of Europe's liveliest party cities.
music: Serbia's most distinctive event is the Guča Trumpet Festival — each year tens of thousands of musicians gather to play feverish Balkan rhythms on brass, the world's grandest brass carnival. The traditional 'kolo' circle dance is inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
In the classical realm, Serbia's Belgrade Philharmonic Orchestra and operatic tradition are long-standing, while Balkan 'turbo-folk' enjoys broad influence within and beyond the region.

musicians.name: Guča Trumpet Festival
musicians.desc: The world's most famous brass festival, hailed as the 'wildest music festival'.

radios.name: Radio Belgrade 2
radios.note: The cultural channel of Serbian broadcasting, also airing classical music.

slovakia.name: Slovakia
slovakia.intro: A land of folk song beneath the Tatra Mountains, with the far-reaching echo of the fujara flute.
history: Slovakia lies in Central Europe; its capital, Bratislava, sits on the Danube, forming a 'Central European triangle' with Vienna and Budapest. It once formed Czechoslovakia with the Czech lands, gaining independence in 1993 after the 'Velvet Divorce'.
The snow-capped peaks of the High Tatras, wooden churches and medieval castles form the country's natural and cultural backdrop.
music: Slovakia's most distinctive folk music is the 'fujara' — a shepherd's flute up to two meters long with a deep tone, inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list. In the classical realm, the Slovak Philharmonic and the Bratislava Music Festival hold considerable sway in Central Europe.

musicians.name: Slovak Philharmonic
musicians.desc: Slovakia's principal classical orchestra, based in Bratislava.

radios.name: RTVS Rádio Devín
radios.note: The cultural channel of Slovak Radio and Television.

slovenia.name: Slovenia
slovenia.intro: Where the Alps meet the Mediterranean, home to Oberkrainer folk music and industrial rock alike.
history: Slovenia lies at the meeting point of the Alps, the Mediterranean and the Pannonian Plain, with extraordinarily diverse landscapes — from the island church of Lake Bled to the Adriatic old town of Piran. Once the most developed part of Yugoslavia, it was the first to gain independence in 1991.
Ljubljana is hailed as one of Europe's most livable green capitals, where culture and nature coexist in harmony.
music: Slovenia's most famous musician is Slavko Avsenik, whose pioneering 'Oberkrainer' folk dance music swept the German-speaking world; the avant-garde industrial band Laibach is internationally known for its provocative artistry.
The Slovenian Philharmonic has a long history (tracing back to 1701) and is one of Europe's oldest musical institutions.

musicians.name: Slavko Avsenik
musicians.desc: The pioneer of Oberkrainer folk music, whose accordion ensembles swept the entire German-speaking world.

musicians.name: Laibach
musicians.desc: A highly avant-garde industrial/experimental band known for its political and artistic provocation.

spain.name: Spain
spain.intro: A land of flamenco and the guitar, and the home of Falla, Domingo and Casals.
history: Spain is one of Europe's most passionate cultural lands: from the Moorish Alhambra to the Gothic cathedrals, and from Gaudí's Barcelona to the flamenco of Seville, everywhere is filled with intense and exuberant art.
During the Age of Discovery, Spain was a global empire; Spanish is now the second most widely spoken mother tongue, and its musical culture radiates across Latin America.
music: Flamenco is Spain's most recognizable music: guitar, song (cante) and dance fused into one, passionate and mournful, and inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The classical guitar tradition is equally glorious — Andrés Segovia and Paco de Lucía elevated the guitar from a folk instrument to the protagonist of the concert stage.

In classical music, Spain has produced composers such as Falla, Albéniz, Granados and Rodrigo (Concierto de Aranjuez), as well as cellist Casals, pianist Larrocha, and Domingo and Carreras of the Three Tenors.

musicians.name: Manuel de Falla
musicians.desc: A leading figure of Spanish nationalism, whose El amor brujo and Nights in the Gardens of Spain glow with vivid color.

musicians.name: Joaquín Rodrigo
musicians.desc: His Concierto de Aranjuez is the most famous guitar concerto in history.

musicians.name: Pablo Casals
musicians.desc: One of the greatest cellists of the 20th century, and a symbol of democracy and humanity.

musicians.name: Plácido Domingo
musicians.desc: One of the Three Tenors, also a noted conductor and opera administrator.

musicians.name: Paco de Lucía
musicians.desc: A legend who brought flamenco guitar to the world, a master of both technique and emotion.

sweden.name: Sweden
sweden.intro: A super-factory of ABBA and pop music, and a Scandinavian kingdom of melody.
history: Sweden is the largest country in Northern Europe; Stockholm, made up of fourteen islands, is called the Venice of the North. Once a great Nordic power in the 17th century, it is now renowned for its welfare system, design and innovation.
From the Nobel Prize to IKEA, from Spotify to H&M, Sweden has deeply shaped the culture, technology and lifestyle of the modern world.
music: Sweden is a pop superpower: groups such as ABBA and Roxette swept the world, while the mastermind Max Martin is among the producers behind the most Billboard No. 1 singles. Stockholm's pop industry is hailed as the Swedish music miracle.
Classical and jazz are equally solid: the Romantic composer Franz Berwald, the pianist Wilhelm Stenhammar, and the legendary jazz trio Esbjörn Svensson Trio (E.S.T.) all add depth to Swedish music.

switzerland.name: Switzerland
switzerland.intro: A diverse Alpine nation and the eternal stage of the Montreux Jazz Festival.
history: Switzerland is known for its Alps, lakes and precision watchmaking; its multilingual culture — German, French, Italian and Romansh — is its distinctive hallmark. Long neutral, it is home to many international organizations in Geneva and Zurich.
The Swiss are rational, precise and nature-loving, a temperament reflected in their rigorous yet diverse musical life.
music: Switzerland's most world-renowned musical event is the Montreux Jazz Festival — a legendary stage on the shores of Lake Geneva where countless jazz and rock masters have left classic performances. In classical music, Switzerland has produced composers such as Bloch, Honegger and Frank Martin, and the conductor Ansermet.
The Lucerne Festival and the Tonhalle-Orchester Zürich are likewise pillars of the European classical scene.

ukraine.name: Ukraine
ukraine.intro: A land of the bandura and Cossack songs, and the birthplace of Horowitz.
history: Ukraine is the second-largest country in Europe by area; Kyiv is the cradle of East Slavic civilization, and Saint Sophia Cathedral and the Monastery of the Caves bear witness to a thousand-year Orthodox tradition. Long part of Tsarist Russia and the Soviet Union, it gained independence in 1991.
Ukraine's black earth is the breadbasket of Europe, while the Cossack cavalry, embroidery (vyshyvanka) and Orthodox icons make up its vivid national memory.
music: Ukrainian folk music is known for the bandura (a plucked string instrument) and polyphonic choral singing, while the Cossack epic ballads (duma) are solemn and vast. In classical music, the piano master Vladimir Horowitz was born in Kyiv, and the composer Valentin Silvestrov is celebrated for his quiet, poetic postlude style.
Its opera tradition is equally deep, and the opera houses of Kyiv and Lviv hold great weight in the Slavic world.

united-kingdom.name: United Kingdom
united-kingdom.intro: The land of the BBC Proms and the Beatles, a twin empire of classical and rock.
history: The United Kingdom comprises England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. It once built the empire on which the sun never set, and the English language and British culture have profoundly shaped the modern world. Big Ben, Tower Bridge and the West End theatres of London are its landmarks.
From Shakespeare to Newton, from the Industrial Revolution to constitutional monarchy, the United Kingdom is a world centre in literature, science, politics and music.
music: British classical music has deep roots: from the Baroque Purcell, to the Romantic Elgar (Pomp and Circumstance Marches), Vaughan Williams and Holst (The Planets), to the 20th-century Britten, British composers hold a distinguished place in Western music. The BBC Proms is the world's largest classical music festival.

In pop and rock, the Beatles, the Rolling Stones, Queen and Pink Floyd defined modern popular music; BBC Radio 3 is widely regarded as one of the finest classical and cultural radio stations in the world.

georgia.name: Georgia
georgia.intro: A land of polyphonic chant in the Caucasus and the ancient home of wine and polyphonic singing.
history: Georgia lies on the southern slopes of the Caucasus, the legendary land of the Golden Fleece and one of the earliest winemaking countries in the world (with some 8,000 years of history). Tbilisi's sulphur baths, ancient churches and wooden-balconied houses are full of oriental romance.

The Georgian language has its own unique alphabet, and its polyphonic singing tradition is inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity — one of the most beautiful vocal legacies of the Orthodox world.
music: Georgian folk polyphony (especially male three-part singing) is world-famous for its miraculously dissonant yet harmonious sound and is listed by UNESCO as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity. In classical music, the composer Zakaria Paliashvili wrote Georgia's first national opera, while the bass Paata Burchuladze is active on the world's opera stages.

musicians.desc: The founder of Georgian national opera; his opera Daisi is a national classic.

armenia.name: Armenia
armenia.intro: The world's first Christian nation and the mournful home of Khachaturian and the duduk.
history: Armenia was the first country to adopt Christianity as its state religion (in 301 AD), and its apostolic churches and monasteries are scattered across its mountains and gorges. Situated at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, it was repeatedly conquered by empires yet always preserved its distinct language, alphabet and cultural identity.
Armenia's tragedy and resilience — above all the genocide of the early 20th century — are deeply imprinted on its art, giving its music a distinctive mournfulness and depth.
music: The soulful voice of Armenia is the duduk — an apricot-wood double-reed flute whose sobbing tone is inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and which the master Djivan Gasparyan carried to the world. In classical music, Aram Khachaturian's Sabre Dance and Spartacus are grand and powerful, while the musicologist Komitas systematically collected Armenian folk songs and is revered as the father of national music.

azerbaijan.name: Azerbaijan
azerbaijan.intro: The Land of Fire and the home of mugham, the birthplace of Eastern opera on the Caspian shore.
history: Azerbaijan means the Land of Fire, and the natural fires and mud volcanoes around Baku are world-famous. Situated on the western shore of the Caspian Sea, it was a key point on the Silk Road where Persian, Turkic and Russian cultures met.
The juxtaposition of Baku's Old City and the Flame Towers is a microcosm of this energy-rich nation's blend of past and present.
music: Azerbaijani mugham is a highly improvisational classical tradition inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, fusing poetry, melody and subtle microtones. In 1908, Uzeyir Hajibeyov's Leyli and Majnun became the first opera in the Islamic world.
In classical music, composers such as Fikret Amirov and Gara Garayev combined national material with modern techniques, while the baritone Muslim Magomayev was a superstar of the Soviet era.

musicians.desc: Composer of Leyli and Majnun, the first opera in the Islamic world, and the founder of modern Azerbaijani music.

musicians.desc: One of the most popular singers of the Soviet era, with a magnificent baritone and star charisma.

vatican-city.name: Vatican City
vatican-city.intro: The world's smallest sovereign state, with the celestial music of the Sistine Chapel and St. Peter's Basilica.
history: Vatican City State is the smallest sovereign state in the world and the centre of the Catholic Church; St. Peter's Basilica and the Sistine Chapel (with Michelangelo's ceiling frescoes) are pinnacles of human art history.
This is the home of Gregorian chant, and the papal choir's history reaches back to the 6th century.
music: The Vatican is inseparable from the Catholic musical tradition: Gregorian chant is one of the earliest written traditions of Western music, and in the 16th century Palestrina served as composer to the papal choir, his polyphonic sacred music becoming a model of Renaissance music. The Sistine Chapel Choir remains one of the oldest choirs in the world.

musicians.name: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina
musicians.desc: A master of Renaissance polyphonic sacred music, whose masses and motets influenced Western music for centuries.

musicians.desc: The Pope's own choir and one of the oldest choral ensembles in the world.
