china.name: China
china.intro: A land of ritual and music, the Eastern source of the pentatonic scale, bronze bells and the guqin, and the classical voice of Shanghai and Harbin.
history: China is one of the world's oldest and longest continuous civilizations, and its musical tradition is ancient: from the ritual-music system of the pre-Qin era, to the majestic bronze-bell sound of the Marquis Yi of Zeng's chime bells, to the elegant silk-and-bamboo timbres of the guqin, pipa and erhu, music has always been bound to the philosophy of rite and harmony.

For generations, scholars cultivated themselves through the qin, chess, calligraphy and painting, and the art of the guqin is inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity; meanwhile, opera forms such as Peking opera and Kunqu fused singing, recitation, acting and martial arts into the pinnacle of Eastern stagecraft.
music: The bedrock of Chinese music is the "blank space" rooted in philosophy and poetry. From the "great sound is rarefied" of the guqin strings to the ink-wash spirit of operatic singing, Chinese classical music never pursues the fullest physical sonority, but looks inward, seeking a state of mind that is at once expansive and subtle.

In the twentieth century, this ancient soundscape met Western symphonic music in a profound collision. The founding of the Shanghai Public Band (forerunner of the Shanghai Symphony Orchestra) in 1879 marked the arrival of the Western classical system in China. Yet Chinese musicians never settled for being mere imitators of Western technique. For nearly a century, generations of composers and performers have pursued a difficult and fascinating quest: to carry the artistic conception of Chinese literati painting on the skeleton of Western instruments, and to translate the depth of Eastern philosophy through the grand textures of the symphony. From the early pioneers who sought the flavour of the flute and guqin on the piano, to today's masters who reshape the Book of Songs and Tang poetry through the symphony in the world's finest concert halls, the history of Chinese music is not only an epic of national awakening, but a century-long aesthetic dialogue between Eastern and Western civilisations.

musicians.name: Guan Pinghu
musicians.role: Qin master, the supreme realm of traditional Chinese literati music
musicians.desc: Signature work: Flowing Water. To understand the wellspring of Chinese music one must listen to the guqin. Guan Pinghu was the most important guqin master of twentieth-century China, with a technique at once archaic and vigorous, and a profound, expansive breath. In 1977, his performance of Flowing Water was engraved on the Voyager 1 Golden Record and sent into space, representing the echo of human civilisation across the cosmos. It is not merely music, but an acoustic expression of the ancient Chinese cosmology of "the unity of Heaven and humanity".

musicians.name: Huang Zi
musicians.role: Composer, founder of modern Chinese professional music education
musicians.desc: A pioneer who perfectly fused Western compositional technique with Chinese poetry. Signature work: The Song of Everlasting Sorrow. Amid the upheaval of the early twentieth century, Huang Zi wrote China's first large-scale orchestral cantata with the highest academic rigour, setting Bai Juyi's tragic love story of the great Tang dynasty to the strict harmony of the Austro-German Romantic tradition — an elegant monument in the history of Chinese symphonic music.

musicians.name: Ma Sicong
musicians.role: Violinist / Composer, pioneer of Chinese violin art
musicians.desc: Hailed as "China's first violinist". Signature work: Nostalgia. With a single Western violin, Ma Sicong drew out the most mellow Chinese homesickness, blending the desolate melody of an Inner Mongolian folk song with the soft tone of the classical violin. In the war-torn years, this piece became a spiritual anchor for countless overseas travellers and intellectuals.

musicians.name: Fou Ts'ong
musicians.role: Pianist, a world-renowned titan of the piano
musicians.desc: Hailed by Time magazine as "the greatest living poet of the piano". Signature works: Chopin's Nocturnes and Mazurkas. Fou Ts'ong's greatness lies in playing Western classics with the soul of a Chinese scholar-official. He infused the poetry of Li Bai, Du Fu and Li Qingzhao, and the "interplay of void and substance" of Chinese ink painting, flawlessly into Chopin's keys — one of the very few Eastern interpreters to win the wholehearted respect of the proud European classical world.

musicians.name: Chen Qigang
musicians.role: Composer, a contemporary master celebrated worldwide
musicians.desc: The last pupil of the great French modernist composer Olivier Messiaen. Signature work: Reflet d'un temps disparu. If anyone could fuse the iridescent colours of French Impressionism with the plaintive beauty of traditional Chinese culture to perfection, it is Chen Qigang. In this cello concerto, he uses the ancient melody Three Variations on the Plum Blossom as a hidden thread, and through a world-class symphonic language expresses with supreme refinement the Eastern meditation on the passage of time and the fragility of life.

japan.name: Japan
japan.intro: The ancient sounds of gagaku and shakuhachi, and the Eastern modern voice of Takemitsu and Sakamoto.
history: Japan is the land of the chrysanthemum and the sword: on one hand it possesses exquisitely refined classical traditions such as gagaku, noh and kabuki, and on the other it influences the world with its intense modernity and popular culture. From the ritual music introduced by envoys to Tang China to the townspeople's culture of the Edo period, music has always run through its aesthetics.
Japan's aesthetics of mono no aware and yūgen have deeply shaped its musical temperament — restrained, full of empty space, and lingering long after the sound fades.
music: Japan's traditional music is vast: court gagaku, rooted in Tang-dynasty banquet music, has been passed down intact for a thousand years; the shakuhachi, shamisen and koto, together with noh and kabuki, make up its universe of sound. After the Meiji Restoration, Japan swiftly embraced Western music and now possesses world-class orchestras and music education.

In the 20th century, Toru Takemitsu combined Japanese aesthetics with avant-garde technique to become an internationally acclaimed master, while Ryuichi Sakamoto moved the world with his scores for The Last Emperor and Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence. In pop, J-pop and anime music are likewise global phenomena.

musicians.name: Toru Takemitsu
musicians.desc: Japan's most important modern composer, uniting Eastern stillness with Western avant-garde technique.

musicians.name: Ryuichi Sakamoto
musicians.desc: Oscar-winning composer for The Last Emperor and former YMO member, whose music spans electronic, classical and film.

musicians.name: Seiji Ozawa
musicians.desc: The first Asian conductor to lead a top world orchestra, long-time music director of the Boston Symphony Orchestra.

musicians.name: Joe Hisaishi
musicians.desc: The signature composer for Hayao Miyazaki's animation, whose melodies for Castle in the Sky and Spirited Away are deeply cherished.

south-korea.name: South Korea
south-korea.intro: A land of pansori and K-pop, with the vibrant new life of Isang Yun and Seoul's classical scene.
history: South Korea has a long musical tradition: from court ritual music to the sung epics of pansori, and from farmers' music (nongak) to shamanic music, the soundscape of the Korean Peninsula is extraordinarily rich. Pansori is inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
Seoul preserves ancient palaces such as Gyeongbokgung while also being a global centre of K-pop and technology, where tradition and the future collide fiercely.
music: South Korea's gugak (national music) is a complete system, with the gayageum, geomungo and daegeum producing distinctive timbres. In Western classical music, the composer Isang Yun is one of Asia's most important composers of the 20th century, fusing Korean aesthetics with European avant-garde technique.
But what truly swept Korean music across the globe is K-pop: from BTS to BLACKPINK, the Korean idol industry has redefined how pop music is produced and spread.

musicians.name: Isang Yun
musicians.desc: One of the most important Asian composers of the 20th century, who wove Korean traditional aesthetics into Western avant-garde music.

musicians.name: Kyung Wha Chung
musicians.desc: A world-class violinist known for her fiery playing and profound interpretation.

musicians.name: Seong-Jin Cho
musicians.desc: Winner of the 2015 International Chopin Piano Competition and one of the most watched young pianists of today.

musicians.name: 防弹少年团

turkey.name: Turkey
turkey.intro: A land of makam at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, and the home of Fazıl Say's crossover piano.
history: Turkey straddles Europe and Asia; Istanbul (formerly Constantinople) was the capital of both the Byzantine and Ottoman empires, where Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque stand side by side as symbols of the meeting of Eastern and Western civilizations.
Centuries of Ottoman rule gave Turkish music, architecture and cuisine the depth of Persian, Arab and Byzantine traditions, while modern secular reforms injected a strong sense of modernity.
music: Turkish classical music centres on the makam system, whose subtle microtones and improvised taksim solos are captivating; the Ottoman military band (mehter) is considered the oldest military band in the world. In folk music, the saz and the aşık (ashik) minstrel tradition have deep roots.

Modern Turkish music is highly eclectic: pianists Fazıl Say and İdil Biret enjoy international renown, while Anatolian rock and Turkish-wave DJs have carried traditional scales into pop and electronic music.

iran.name: Iran
iran.intro: The thousand-year home of Persian classical music (radif) and the poetry of the santur and tar.
history: Iran is the heir of Persian civilization, with more than 2,500 years of history; the ruins of Persepolis and the mosques of Isfahan bear witness to past glory. Persian poetry (Hafez, Rumi), miniature painting and Persian carpets together form its refined spiritual world.
Persian culture is known for its elegance; poetry and music blend seamlessly, forming one of the oldest and most mature artistic traditions of the Islamic world.
music: Persian classical music centres on the radif (a repertoire of melodic modes) and the dastgah (modal system), using instruments such as the santur, tar, kamancheh and ney, with improvisation inseparable from poetic recitation. This tradition is inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

Since the 20th century, the vocal master Mohammad-Reza Shajarian, the kamancheh master Kayhan Kalhor and the tar player Hossein Alizadeh have carried Persian classical music to the world, becoming the proudest calling cards of Iranian culture.

india.name: India
india.intro: The sacred tradition of raga and tala, and an empire of sitar and Bollywood song-and-dance.
history: India is one of the world's four great ancient civilizations, and music here is given a divine origin (said to spring from Vedic chant). The Hindu concept of Nada Brahma (sound is Brahman) keeps music forever bound to religion, philosophy and meditation.
A country of over a billion people and hundreds of languages, its cultural diversity and depth are unmatched in the world.
music: Indian classical music is divided into the northern Hindustani and southern Carnatic systems, centred on raga (melodic framework) and tala (rhythmic cycle), and filled with subtle improvisation. The sitar master Ravi Shankar, the sarod master Ali Akbar Khan and the tabla master Zakir Hussain carried this tradition to the West.
Alongside the classical tradition runs the vast Bollywood song-and-dance industry, whose film songs permeate everyday Indian life with an output and reach rarely seen anywhere in the world.

thailand.name: Thailand
thailand.intro: The Land of Smiles and the home of piphat court music and luk thung country song.
history: Thailand is the only Southeast Asian country never colonized, known as the Land of Smiles. Bangkok's Grand Palace and Temple of the Emerald Buddha are resplendent, and Buddhist culture pervades every corner of life.
Thai tradition is inseparable from royal ritual; court music and dance, floating markets and the Songkran water festival together form its colourful folk panorama.
music: Thai classical music is typified by the piphat ensemble, in which the ranat (xylophone), gong circle and pi (oboe) produce a splendid, ritualistic court sound. In the folk realm, luk thung (country song) and mor lam (northeastern sung poetry) are two popular traditions, heartfelt and down-to-earth.
The classical Thai dance-drama khon fuses masked dance, music and the epic Ramakien, and is one of the highest forms of Thai art.

musicians.name: Thai Royal Court Ensemble
musicians.desc: A court music group carrying on the piphat ensemble tradition.

musicians.name: Phum Viphurit
musicians.desc: A representative of Thailand's new generation of indie music, reaching the international stage with fresh bedroom pop.

vietnam.name: Vietnam
vietnam.intro: A land of the monochord and quan họ folk songs, with the melodious call-and-response of the Red River Delta.
history: Vietnam is deeply influenced by Chinese civilization yet distinctly individual; Hanoi's Temple of Literature, the Nguyễn-dynasty Imperial City of Huế and the ancient town of Hội An bear witness to thousands of years of history. It is the rice bowl of Southeast Asia, where the Red River and Mekong deltas nourish a splendid rice-growing civilization.
Vietnamese culture rests on a foundation of Confucianism, Buddhism and Taoism, blended with Cham, Khmer and other diverse elements.
music: Vietnam's most distinctive instrument is the monochord (đàn bầu), which with a single string produces sobbing, sliding tones. The quan họ love-song duets and ca trù chanting of the north, and the nhạc tài tử music of the south, are all inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
Contemporary V-pop and cover culture flourish among the younger generation.

musicians.desc: A national institution carrying on Vietnamese traditional music such as the monochord and quan họ.

indonesia.name: Indonesia
indonesia.intro: The gamelan of a thousand islands, the deep resonance of bronze gongs and bamboo music.
history: Indonesia comprises more than 17,000 islands, the world's largest archipelagic nation. Java, Bali, Sumatra and other islands nurtured highly developed court and folk cultures, and Borobudur and Prambanan temples are monuments to its ancient civilization.
Diverse ethnic groups and religions (Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Christianity) give Indonesian culture astonishing richness.
music: Gamelan is Indonesia's greatest musical legacy — an ensemble of bronze gongs, gong-chimes and percussion whose metallic resonance and cyclic rhythms are as profound as the cosmos. Inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, it also deeply influenced Western composers such as Debussy.
In folk music, kroncong and dangdut are respectively Indonesia's nostalgic love songs and its most popular dance music.

malaysia.name: Malaysia
malaysia.intro: A harmony of diverse peoples, the symphony of Malay ghazal, Chinese orchestra and Indian music.
history: Malaysia consists of the Malay Peninsula and northern Borneo, a diverse society where Malay, Chinese and Indian communities coexist harmoniously. Kuala Lumpur's Petronas Towers and the old city of Melaka symbolize its modern and historical faces.
Islamic, Chinese and Indian cultures intertwine here, shaping an extraordinarily rich musical ecology.
music: Malay traditional music includes ghazal, the dikir barat chorus and the traditional joget dance tunes of Johor; at the same time, Chinese orchestral music and Indian classical and Tamil film music also flourish in Malaysia, forming a unique multicultural harmony.

musicians.name: Malaysian Philharmonic Orchestra
musicians.desc: Resident at the Petronas Concert Hall beneath the Twin Towers in Kuala Lumpur, one of Southeast Asia's best-known symphony orchestras.

philippines.name: Philippines
philippines.intro: The kundiman love song and rondalla ensemble, an archipelago of born singers.
history: The Philippines comprises more than 7,000 islands and, after over three centuries of Spanish and several decades of American colonization, became the most Westernized country in Asia. Manila's Intramuros and its Baroque churches bear witness to this complex history.
The blend of Catholic faith, Spanish love-song tradition and American popular culture has forged the Philippines' distinctive musical character.
music: The kundiman is the traditional Filipino love song, its melody tender and plaintive, often sung as a serenade (harana) to one's beloved; the rondalla is a Spanish-style plucked-string ensemble. Filipinos are enormously gifted singers, and the country has one of the highest densities of singers in the world.

singapore.name: Singapore
singapore.intro: A garden city where East meets West, the stage of Esplanade and the Singapore Symphony.
history: Singapore is a city-state in Southeast Asia that grew from a fishing village into a global financial and trade centre. Known as a garden city, it counts Marina Bay Sands and the Supertrees among its modern landmarks.
Chinese, Malay, Indian and Eurasian cultures coexist here, with English as the common language, fostering a highly international artistic ecology.
music: Singapore's music scene is diverse and refined: the Singapore Symphony Orchestra is among Southeast Asia's finest, and the Esplanade (the durian-shell theatre) hosts world-class performances year-round. Chinese orchestral music (the Singapore Chinese Orchestra) and Malay and Indian traditional music also flourish side by side.

myanmar.name: Myanmar
myanmar.intro: A land of golden pagodas, with the ancient echo of the hsaing waing ensemble and the harp.
history: Myanmar is famous for Bagan, the city of ten thousand pagodas, where thousands of stupas dot the plains along the Irrawaddy River — one of Southeast Asia's most spectacular religious landscapes. Once a powerful kingdom on the Indochinese Peninsula, it is deeply influenced by Theravada Buddhism.
Myanmar's traditional culture is inseparable from Buddhist ritual, and its music, dance and drama largely serve religion and the court.
music: Myanmar's traditional hsaing waing ensemble centres on a circle of tuned drums, accompanied by gongs, oboes and other instruments, with passionate and complex rhythms; the Burmese harp (saung-gauk), an ancient instrument unique to Southeast Asia, has a pure, refined tone and symbolizes court and literati music.

musicians.desc: Myanmar's most representative drum ensemble, often used at festivals and ceremonies.

cambodia.name: Cambodia
cambodia.intro: The smile of Angkor, the pinpeat court music and the dance of the apsaras.
history: Cambodia is the heartland of the ancient Khmer Empire; Angkor Wat and the Khmer smile of the Bayon are marvels of architectural history. The court music and dance of this once-dominant civilization are still treasured as national gems.
Khmer classical dance (the apsara dance) and the pinpeat ensemble are inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
music: The pinpeat is Cambodia's court ceremonial ensemble, its xylophones, gong-circle and drums entwined with the apsara dance in splendour and solemnity. Folk music includes the chapei dang veng (long-necked lute) sung poetry and mahori chamber music.

musicians.desc: A Cambodian royal ensemble carrying on the pinpeat and apsara dance traditions.

radios.note: Cambodia's national radio, broadcasting traditional music.

laos.name: Laos
laos.intro: A serene Buddhist land on the Mekong, with the melodious harmony of the khaen bamboo mouth organ.
history: Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia; the Mekong runs through it, and the old city and temples of Luang Prabang make it a tranquil Buddhist haven. Once the land of the Lan Xang kingdom, it was later influenced by its neighbours and France.
Life in Laos moves at a gentle pace, and the harmony of Buddhism and nature permeates its music.
music: Laos' most representative instrument is the khaen, a mouth organ made of bamboo tubes with a clear, melodious tone, the soul of mor lam folk song and rural life. Khaen music is inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

musicians.desc: Lao folk music centred on the bamboo mouth organ khaen, melodious and intimate.

radios.note: Lao national radio, broadcasting local and traditional music.

brunei.name: Brunei
brunei.intro: A wealthy sultanate in Borneo, with the quiet echo of Malay court music.
history: Brunei is a small country on the island of Borneo, known for the wealth brought by oil and gas; its sultan is among the richest monarchs in the world. The water villages and golden-domed mosque of the capital Bandar Seri Begawan are distinctive.
As a member of the Islamic Malay cultural sphere, Brunei's traditional music is closely tied to the Malay court and Islamic ritual.
music: Brunei's traditional music features the Malay court gulintangan (xylophone ensemble) and Islamic chanting (such as Kelantanese-style zikir), often accompanied by frame drums and gong ensembles at weddings and festivals.

musicians.name: Gulintangan Ensemble
musicians.desc: A percussion ensemble of the Brunei Malay court, often used in royal and festive ceremonies.

radios.name: Radio Television Brunei

timor-leste.name: Timor-Leste
timor-leste.intro: Asia's youngest nation, where Tetum sacred houses meet Catholic sacred music and echoes of fado.
history: Timor-Leste occupies the eastern half of the island of Timor and is one of Asia's youngest and most long-suffering nations. Colonized by Portugal for nearly 450 years, it briefly declared independence after Portugal's withdrawal in 1975, only to be occupied by Indonesia for twenty-four years until formally restoring its independence on 20 May 2002.

Catholic faith (a legacy of Portuguese colonization) and indigenous Tetum culture are deeply interwoven here: the uma lulik (sacred houses) of the mountains are the spiritual centres of communities, while coastal fishing villages and rugged highlands form the unadorned backdrop of this young nation.
music: Timor-Leste's music is inseparable from ritual, dance and oral tradition. The traditional song-and-dance tebedai, centred on circle drumming and antiphonal singing, is performed at weddings, harvests and celebrations; indigenous instruments are chiefly drums (babadok), bamboo flutes and strings. Portuguese colonization brought the Catholic sacred-music tradition, and parish choirs in Dili are still known for four-part chant, with the melancholy strains of fado occasionally heard.

The Indonesian occupation (1975–1999) let dangdut and Indonesian pop seep into local life, mingling with indigenous Tetum music and Portuguese melodies. The national anthem Pátria (Fatherland) was written by the poet Francisco Borja da Costa and composed by Afonso Redentor Araújo; its lyricist was tragically killed during the Indonesian invasion, making the song an emblem of this nation's memory of independence.

musicians.desc: Lyricist of Timor-Leste's national anthem Pátria, killed during the Indonesian invasion and revered as a martyr and symbol of the independence movement.

musicians.name: Afonso Redentor Araújo
musicians.desc: Composer of Pátria, whose melody became the sound of Timor-Leste's national awakening.

musicians.name: Tebedai Ensemble
musicians.desc: A Timorese traditional song-and-dance form centred on circle drumming and antiphonal singing, common at weddings and celebrations.

mongolia.name: Mongolia
mongolia.intro: A grassland country of the morin khuur and khöömei, and the far-reaching long song of a nomadic people.
history: Mongolia is the homeland of the vast empire founded by Genghis Khan, where broad steppe and desert shaped a nomadic way of life. The ger (yurt), the Naadam festival and herds of horses are the country's enduring cultural symbols.
Nomadic life keeps Mongolian music forever bound to nature, horses and the boundless land, and its sound carries a desolate yet free sense of vastness.
music: Mongolia's most recognizable music is khöömei (overtone singing, in which one voice produces several pitches at once) and the morin khuur (a two-stringed fiddle with a horse-head scroll and a neighing tone), both inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The long song (urtiin duu) sings the boundlessness of the steppe in long, sustained melody.
Contemporary Mongolia has both tradition-keeping ensembles in Ulaanbaatar and bands such as The HU, which combine khöömei with rock and have reached the international stage.

musicians.name: Mongolian State Morin Khuur Ensemble
musicians.desc: A state ensemble carrying on the morin khuur and khöömei traditions, with a vast and desolate tone.

musicians.name: The HU
musicians.desc: A band fusing Mongolian khöömei and the morin khuur with heavy metal, popular worldwide.

radios.name: MNB 蒙古国家广播
radios.note: Mongolian National Broadcaster, airing long song and local music programs.

north-korea.name: North Korea
north-korea.intro: A land of Juche art and traditional gugak, the stage of the Moranbong Band and the Unhasu Orchestra.
history: North Korea occupies the northern Korean Peninsula and shares an ancient nationhood with South Korea. Pyongyang's Mangyongdae, the Juche Tower and the Chollima statue form this country's distinctive political and cultural landscape.
North Korea's traditional music shares the same roots as the south — court music, pansori and folk songs — while also developing a distinctive Juche-art style.
music: North Korean gugak centres on the gayageum, geomungo and folk songs, sharing its roots with South Korea's gugak. In Western classical music, Pyongyang has large ensembles such as the Moranbong Band and the Unhasu Orchestra, and a complete system of music education.
North Korea's musical output centres on themes of nation and revolution, grand in scale and intense in emotion, forming an important part of its national narrative.

musicians.name: Moranbong Band
musicians.desc: North Korea's best-known all-female ensemble, fusing symphonic, electronic and folk music.

musicians.name: Isang Yun
musicians.desc: A composer born on the Korean Peninsula who, though long resident in Europe, profoundly influenced modern East Asian music.

north-korea.radioNote: North Korea's national broadcaster (Korean Central Broadcasting) currently has no publicly accessible online music stream, so online listening is not yet available.

kazakhstan.name: Kazakhstan
kazakhstan.intro: A great steppe nation of the dombra and küy, and Central Asia's vast musical heartland.
history: Kazakhstan is the largest country in Central Asia, spanning the vast Eurasian steppe. The nomadic Kazakhs take pride in horsemanship and archery, and their land was an important corridor of the Silk Road.
Soviet-era industrialization and the modern construction of the new capital Astana give this steppe country both a traditional and a modern face.
music: Kazakhstan's most representative instrument is the dombra, a two-stringed plucked instrument with a clear, bright tone; the küy is an instrumental piece for dombra that often tells a story through music. The improvised aitys duels of the akyn (bard) are also part of its oral literary tradition.
Kazakhstan has Central Asia's most complete classical music system, with strong opera houses and symphony orchestras in Almaty and Astana.

musicians.name: Kurmangazy Sagyrbayuly
musicians.desc: Kazakhstan's greatest dombra player and composer, whose küy works are still performed today.

musicians.name: Dina Nurpeisova
musicians.desc: A Kazakh female dombra master in the Kurmangazy tradition, of extraordinary skill.

radios.name: Kazakh Radio / Radio Classic
radios.note: Kazakh national radio and classical music channel, broadcasting dombra and symphonic music.

uzbekistan.name: Uzbekistan
uzbekistan.intro: A treasure of Shashmaqom and the Silk Road, and the musical echo of Samarkand.
history: Uzbekistan is the heart of the Silk Road; the ancient cities of Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva were the glorious centres of the Timurid Empire and the Khanate of Bukhara, and their blue-domed mosques and madrasas are world-famous.
As Central Asia's most populous country, Uzbekistan has a deep Perso-Turkic cultural heritage, and its music, miniature painting and carpet craft are all extremely refined.
music: Shashmaqom (six maqoms) is a classical musical treasure shared by Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, fusing poetry, voice and instruments and inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The dutar, tanbur and doira (frame drum) are its representative instruments.
Uzbek opera and ballet developed greatly during the Soviet era, and the Navoi Theatre in Tashkent still stages high-quality performances.

musicians.name: Munojat Yulchieva
musicians.desc: A leading Uzbek female singer of Shashmaqom and Sufi music, with an ethereal, pure voice.

musicians.name: Yulduz Usmonova
musicians.desc: One of Uzbekistan's most popular singers, blending tradition with the contemporary.

radios.name: Uzbekistan Radio
radios.note: Uzbek national radio, broadcasting Shashmaqom and folk music.

kyrgyzstan.name: Kyrgyzstan
kyrgyzstan.intro: A snow-mountain land of the Manas epic and the komuz.
history: Kyrgyzstan lies in the heart of the Tien Shan mountains, where Lake Issyk-Kul gleams like a pearl among the snowy peaks. The nomadic Kyrgyz preserve their national memory through the epic Manas.
This million-line epic is one of the longest in the world and has been inscribed by UNESCO on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
music: Kyrgyz music is inseparable from epic recitation: the manaschi improvise passages of Manas to the accompaniment of the komuz (a three-stringed plucked instrument), a living fossil of nomadic culture. The komuz has a clear tone and elaborate playing technique.

musicians.name: Sayakbay Karalaev
musicians.desc: One of the greatest reciters of Manas in the 20th century, able to chant hundreds of thousands of lines from memory.

radios.name: Kyrgyz Radio
radios.note: Kyrgyz national radio, broadcasting Manas and folk music.

tajikistan.name: Tajikistan
tajikistan.intro: The Persian legacy of the Pamirs, the poetry and music of Shashmaqom and Rudaki.
history: Tajikistan lies in the Pamir Mountains and is the only Persian-speaking former Soviet republic, its cultural lineage reaching back to ancient Persian civilization. The poet Rudaki, hailed as the father of Persian poetry, was born on this land.
The meeting of mountain gorges and the Silk Road gives Tajik music both Persian elegance and highland simplicity.
music: Tajikistan shares the classical treasure Shashmaqom with Uzbekistan, whose refined blend of voice and instruments is inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The Tajik falak is the sorrowful, far-reaching mountain song of the Pamir people.

musicians.name: Rudaki
musicians.desc: The father of Persian poetry, whose poetic-musical tradition laid the spiritual foundation of Tajik and Persian culture.

musicians.name: Academy of Maqom
musicians.desc: A Tajik national institution carrying on the Shashmaqom tradition.

radios.name: Radio Tajikistan
radios.note: Tajik national radio, broadcasting Shashmaqom and Persian music.

turkmenistan.name: Turkmenistan
turkmenistan.intro: A land of the dutar in the Karakum Desert, a city of white marble.
history: Turkmenistan lies in southwestern Central Asia, with the Karakum Desert covering most of its territory. Its capital Ashgabat is known for its white-marble buildings, quite unlike any other.
Turkmenistan's nomadic-oasis culture nurtured a distinctive musical tradition, and the dutar is its most revered instrument.
music: The dutar (two-stringed plucked instrument) and the gijak (bowed string instrument) are the soul of Turkmen music, and the bagshy bards, who sing epics and folk songs to their own dutar accompaniment, form Turkmenistan's most important musical tradition.

musicians.name: Bakshy (Bakhshi) tradition
musicians.desc: A Turkmen bardic tradition of singing epics to one's own dutar, inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

turkmenistan.radioNote: Turkmenistan's broadcasting system is highly closed, and there is currently no publicly accessible online music stream, so online listening is not yet available.

saudi-arabia.name: Saudi Arabia
saudi-arabia.intro: A land of Islamic holy sites and desert song, the voice of the Arabian Peninsula.
history: Saudi Arabia is the birthplace of Islam, and the two holy cities of Mecca and Medina draw millions of pilgrims every year. A kingdom known for desert and oil, it is one of the most influential countries in the Arab world.
Nomadic Bedouin culture and Islamic faith have deeply shaped Saudi music and way of life.
music: Saudi traditional music is best known for the Bedouin Nabati poetry recitation and the Ardah sword dance, the latter inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The oud, rabab and frame drums are the main accompanying instruments.
Although religious tradition once restricted public musical performance, Saudi Arabia has recently been opening its cultural sphere, with music festivals and symphony orchestras flourishing.

musicians.name: Mohammed Abdu
musicians.desc: Known as the Artist of the Arabs, one of Saudi Arabia's most influential singers.

radios.name: Saudi Radio / MBC FM
radios.note: The music channels of Saudi Broadcasting and the MBC Group, airing Arabic music.

yemen.name: Yemen
yemen.intro: A land of Sanaa's old city and Sanaani song, the ancient highlands of the Arabian Peninsula.
history: Yemen lies in the southwest of the Arabian Peninsula and was once the land of the Sabaean kingdom and the Himyarite dynasty. The mud-brick tower houses of Sanaa's old city are a World Heritage site and a gem of Arab architectural history.
Yemen's mountains, gorges and coast have produced diverse folk-music traditions reaching back to the earliest roots of Arab music.
music: Yemen's Sanaani singing is inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, its poetry and melody standing apart in the Arab world. The musical tradition of Yemeni Jews (later carried to Israel through emigration) has had a profound influence on Arab music.
At Yemeni gatherings (qat chews), the oud and poetry recitation are an indispensable part of the occasion.

musicians.name: Ahmed Fathi
musicians.desc: A Yemeni oud master whose playing brims with the deep feeling and improvisation of Arab music.

yemen.radioNote: Years of war have severely damaged Yemen's broadcasting infrastructure, and there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

oman.name: Oman
oman.intro: A maritime civilization of the frankincense land, with Omani traditional music and the Royal Opera House Muscat.
history: Oman lies in the southeast of the Arabian Peninsula and was once a key hub of the maritime spice and frankincense trade, its sailing ships voyaging to the East African coast and across the Indian Ocean to form a distinctive maritime civilization.
Muscat's Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque and the Royal Opera House symbolize its modern face in religion and art respectively.
music: Omani traditional music centres on tribal songs and sword dances such as the razha and al-azi, while the sailors' songs (nima) preserve memories of the age of sail. The Royal Oman Symphony Orchestra and the Royal Opera House represent its embrace of Western classical music.

musicians.name: Royal Oman Symphony Orchestra
musicians.desc: One of the earliest symphony orchestras established on the Arabian Peninsula, resident at the Royal Opera House Muscat.

radios.name: Oman FM / Sultanate of Oman Radio
radios.note: Oman's national radio, broadcasting traditional music and cultural programs.

united-arab-emirates.name: United Arab Emirates
united-arab-emirates.intro: A city of music in the desert, the diverse stage of Dubai Opera.
history: The UAE is made up of seven emirates and rose in just a few decades from pearling villages into a global financial, trade and cultural centre. Dubai's Burj Khalifa and Palm Islands and Abu Dhabi's Louvre outpost are symbols of its ambition.
The country's modernization miracle attracts artists and orchestras from around the world.
music: Traditionally, the UAE is known for the Al-Ayyala stick dance and the pearl-diving songs (nahma), with Al-Ayyala inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Today, Dubai Opera and the Abu Dhabi Festival bring Western classical music and international stars together here.

musicians.name: Hussain Al Jassmi
musicians.desc: The UAE's most representative singer, a household name across the Arab world.

radios.name: Abu Dhabi Classic FM
radios.note: Abu Dhabi's classical music station, one of the few channels in the Gulf dedicated to classical music.

qatar.name: Qatar
qatar.intro: A peninsula of pearls and natural gas, a symphonic oasis of the Qatar Philharmonic.
history: Qatar is a small peninsula nation on the Persian Gulf that ranks among the world's highest-income countries thanks to its natural gas. Doha's Museum of Islamic Art and Education City show its ambition to invest in culture.
Hosting the World Cup and founding the Qatar Philharmonic have brought this small Gulf state to prominence on the cultural and sporting stage.
music: Qatar's traditional music centres on sea shanties and the Ardah sword dance, sharing a Bedouin-maritime culture with its Gulf neighbours. In modern music, the Qatar Philharmonic Orchestra (founded in 2007) is the Arab world's foremost symphony orchestra, regularly collaborating with international conductors.

musicians.name: Qatar Philharmonic Orchestra
musicians.desc: One of the most prestigious symphony orchestras in the Arab world, resident in Doha.

radios.name: Qatar Radio / QBS
radios.note: Qatar radio, broadcasting Arabic and traditional music.

kuwait.name: Kuwait
kuwait.intro: The Gulf home of sawt, and the refined tradition of Arab music.
history: Kuwait lies at the head of the Persian Gulf and was once a centre of the pearl trade and seafaring, now known for its oil wealth. It is also one of the most developed countries in the Gulf in journalism and publishing.
Kuwait's contribution to Arab music — above all the Gulf songs known as sawt and ta'ka — is highly esteemed throughout the Arab world.
music: Kuwait is a major centre of Gulf sawt (a musical form blending African, Indian and Arab elements), whose refined, complex rhythms and improvisation deeply influenced music throughout the Gulf. Many oud masters have emerged here.

musicians.name: Abdul Karim Abdul Qadir
musicians.desc: A legendary singer of Kuwait and the Gulf whose performances influenced several generations.

radios.name: Kuwait Radio
radios.note: Kuwait's national radio, broadcasting Gulf and Arabic music.

bahrain.name: Bahrain
bahrain.intro: A pearl island nation of the Dilmun civilization, the gentle home of Gulf traditional music.
history: Bahrain is an archipelago nation in the Persian Gulf, once the center of the ancient Dilmun civilization; millennia of pearl diving earned it the name "the Pearl of the Gulf."
As one of the earliest and most internationalized countries in the Gulf region, Bahrain's music blends deep Gulf traditions with diverse cultural influences.
music: Bahrain's fidjeri — the work songs of pearl divers — is its unique musical heritage, inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The Gulf's sawt and oud traditions also flourish in Bahrain.

musicians.name: Bahrain Folk Music Ensemble
musicians.desc: A Bahraini music group carrying on the fidjeri pearl-diving songs and Gulf percussion traditions.

radios.name: Bahrain Radio
radios.note: Bahrain's national broadcaster, playing Gulf traditional music.

iraq.name: Iraq
iraq.intro: The home of maqam in the land of two rivers, the golden echoes of the oud and Baghdad.
history: Iraq is the birthplace of the Mesopotamian civilization; Baghdad was once the world's intellectual center during the Abbasid Caliphate, and the tales of One Thousand and One Nights were born here.
The golden age of Arab classical music is inseparable from Baghdad, whose musical tradition is one of the oldest living heritages in the Arab world.
music: Iraqi Maqam, inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, is a refined art form blending poetry, vocals and instruments, regarded as the pinnacle of Arab classical music. Oud masters such as Munir Bashir and Naseer Shamma took this tradition to the world.

musicians.name: Munir Bashir
musicians.desc: Hailed as the "King of the Oud," he brought the Iraqi maqam tradition to the international stage.

musicians.name: Naseer Shamma
musicians.desc: One of the most renowned contemporary oud players, founder of the Arab Oud House.

radios.name: Iraqi Media Network
radios.note: Iraq's national media network, broadcasting Iraqi maqam and Arab music.

syria.name: Syria
syria.intro: The muwashshah songs of Damascus, the refined home of Arab music.
history: Damascus is one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities and was once the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate; its mosques and old city tell of a thousand years of civilization.
Syria is a major center of Arab classical music, and the muwashshah poetic-musical tradition was born here.
music: The muwashshah is Syria's refined Andalusian-Arab poetic music, elegant in melody and intricate in rhythm. Aleppo's Qudud Halabiya songs are inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Oud master Farid al-Atrash and the singer Asmahan both came from Syria.

musicians.name: Farid al-Atrash
musicians.desc: A Syrian-born musical giant whose oud artistry and singing deeply influenced the Arab music world.

musicians.name: Sabah Fakhri
musicians.desc: A master of the Aleppan Qudud Halabiya songs, whose majestic singing moved the entire Arab world.

radios.name: Syrian Radio
radios.note: Syrian broadcasting, playing muwashshah and traditional Arab music.

lebanon.name: Lebanon
lebanon.intro: "Paris of the Middle East," the voices of Fairuz and the Rahbani Brothers.
history: Lebanon was once the center of the Phoenician civilization; with its open culture and vibrant nightlife, Beirut was called the "Paris of the Middle East." It is one of the most Westernized and culturally flourishing countries in the Arab world.
Arab music reached a high synthesis of popularity and refinement in Lebanon, whose recording industry once led the entire Arab world.
music: Lebanon's Fairuz is the most beloved singer in the Arab world; her collaboration with the Rahbani Brothers created the golden age of modern Lebanese music. Lebanon is also a major center of Arab pop, the oud, and the maqam tradition.

musicians.name: Fairuz
musicians.desc: The most iconic singer in the Arab world, hailed as "the voice of Lebanon."

musicians.name: Rahbani Brothers
musicians.desc: Assi and Mansour Rahbani, whose operatic songs written for Fairuz defined modern Arab music.

radios.name: Radio Liban / Voice of Lebanon
radios.note: Radio Liban and the Voice of Lebanon, broadcasting Arab music and cultural programs.

jordan.name: Jordan
jordan.intro: The land of the rose-red city of Petra and Bedouin songs.
history: Jordan is famed for the rose-red ancient city of Petra and the Dead Sea; Petra is listed among the New Seven Wonders of the World. It is a crossroads of the ancient Nabataean civilization and biblical stories.
The nomadic songs of the Bedouin and Arab tradition form the bedrock of Jordanian music.
music: Jordan's folk music centers on the Bedouin hijini riding songs and dahiyya dances, accompanied by the oud, rabab and hand drums. Amman has also seen a lively contemporary music scene emerge in recent years.

musicians.name: Omar Al-Abdallat
musicians.desc: One of Jordan's most representative singers, performing Bedouin and national songs.

radios.name: Jordan Radio
radios.note: Jordan's radio and television, broadcasting Bedouin and Arab music.

israel.name: Israel
israel.intro: The hall of the Philharmonic and a classical stronghold of the Middle East, a symphony of diverse immigrants.
history: Israel lies on the eastern Mediterranean coast, at the meeting point of the holy sites of Judaism, Christianity and Islam. The Western Wall, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the Dome of the Rock stand side by side in Jerusalem's Old City.
The musical traditions brought by Jewish immigrants from around the world collide here into an extraordinarily rich cultural ecosystem.
music: The Israel Philharmonic Orchestra (founded by Huberman in 1936) is one of the world's leading orchestras; masters such as Mehta and Barenboim have worked closely with it. Beyond classical music, Israel's Hebrew songs, klezmer and contemporary electronic music also flourish.

musicians.name: Itzhak Perlman
musicians.desc: One of the greatest living violinists, born in Israel.

musicians.name: Daniel Barenboim
musicians.desc: A musical giant born in Argentina with Israeli citizenship, who promotes Israeli-Palestinian musical cooperation.

musicians.name: Zubin Mehta
musicians.desc: Long-time leader of the Israel Philharmonic Orchestra and its closest artistic partner.

radios.name: Kol HaMusica
radios.note: The classical music channel of Israel's broadcasting.

palestine.name: Palestine
palestine.intro: A land of olive trees and the oud, the deep nostalgia of Palestinian folk song.
history: Palestine lies on the holy land of the eastern Mediterranean coast; ancient cities such as Bethlehem and Hebron carry profound religious and historical memory. Arab culture on this land runs deep.
Despite prolonged turmoil, Palestinian music and poetry have always been the emotional and identity anchor of the people.
music: Palestine's ataba and dalouna folk songs are known for their long improvisations and deep emotion, while the dabke group dance rhythm runs through its festivals. Oud master Simon Shaheen and the singer Kamel Khalil are among those who brought the voice of Palestine to the world.

musicians.name: Simon Shaheen
musicians.desc: A Palestinian-American music master who blends Arab classical music with jazz and Western classical.

musicians.name: Reem Kelani
musicians.desc: A British-Palestinian singer who collects and performs Palestinian folk songs.

radios.name: Voice of Palestine
radios.note: The Voice of Palestine broadcasting, playing Palestinian folk and Arab music.

afghanistan.name: Afghanistan
afghanistan.intro: A land of the rubab and the poetry of Ghazni, a crossroads of the Silk Road.
history: Afghanistan lies at the meeting point of Central and South Asia, once a crossroads of Buddhist, Hellenistic and Islamic civilizations; the remains of the Bamiyan Buddhas testify to its past glory.
This mountainous plateau nurtured diverse peoples and music; it is the homeland of Sufi poets such as Rumi.
music: Afghanistan's national treasure instrument is the rubab (a short-necked lute), whose clear tone is the soul of Afghan music. The ghazal poetic-musical tradition and the Persian-Indian classical fusion meet here.
Regrettably, Afghan music culture has been severely affected by the unrest of recent years.

musicians.name: Ustad Mohammad Omar
musicians.desc: A master of the Afghan rubab whose performances have been widely recorded.

musicians.name: Ahmad Zahir
musicians.desc: Hailed as the "Afghan Elvis," his voice is a shared memory of generations of Afghans.

afghanistan.radioNote: Due to the situation, Afghanistan currently has no stable accessible online music stream, and online playback cannot be provided for the time being.

bangladesh.name: Bangladesh
bangladesh.intro: The home of Tagore and Rabindra Sangeet.
history: Bangladesh lies in the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta and is one of the world's most densely populated countries. It gained independence from Pakistan in 1971, and its national anthem is Tagore's famous work "Amar Shonar Bangla."
Bengali literature and music traditions run deep, and the poetry and music of Rabindranath Tagore are deeply rooted in this land.
music: Rabindra Sangeet (the vast body of songs composed by Tagore) is the soul of Bengali culture, widely sung. Its folk music is most moving in the Baul tradition (mystic minstrels, inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity) and the Bhatiyali (boatmen's songs).

musicians.name: Rabindranath Tagore
musicians.desc: A Nobel laureate in literature who composed thousands of songs and is the soul of Bengali music.

musicians.name: Lalon Shah
musicians.desc: Bengal's greatest mystic poet and singer, whose ideas were profoundly influential.

radios.name: Bangladesh Betar
radios.note: Bangladesh's national broadcaster, playing Rabindra Sangeet and folk music.

bhutan.name: Bhutan
bhutan.intro: The happy kingdom of the Himalayas, the echoes of masked dances and monastic horns.
history: Bhutan lies on the southern slopes of the Himalayas and is world-renowned for its philosophy of Gross National Happiness. It long remained independent and secluded, gradually opening to the world only in the 20th century.
Vajrayana Buddhism has deeply shaped Bhutanese culture; monasteries and festivals are the center of its spiritual life.
music: Bhutan's traditional music centers on Tibetan Buddhist monastic ritual, with the solemn ensemble of dungchen (long horns), gyaling (shawms) and cymbals running through religious festivals. Folk traditions include the cham masked dance and zhabdro song-and-dance.

musicians.name: Bhutanese Monastic Ensemble
musicians.desc: A Bhutanese monastic group performing Tibetan Buddhist ritual music on long horns, shawms and cymbals.

bhutan.radioNote: Bhutan's broadcasting focuses on cultural and religious programs; there is currently no publicly accessible online music stream.

maldives.name: Maldives
maldives.intro: The coral island nation of the Indian Ocean, the oceanic rhythm of Boduberu drumming.
history: The Maldives consists of over a thousand coral islands and is the world's lowest-lying country. It was long a supply stop on Indian Ocean trade routes, deeply influenced by South Asian, Arab and East African cultures.
Its turquoise seas and diving spots make it one of the world's most renowned resort destinations.
music: The Maldives' most distinctive music is Boduberu — percussion music originating in East Africa, featuring large drums and chorus, with fiery rhythms and dance that are the soul of island celebrations.

musicians.name: Boduberu Ensemble
musicians.desc: Maldives' traditional music built on large drums, chorus and dance, passionate and exuberant.

maldives.radioNote: The Maldives' island broadcasting focuses on tourism and general programs; there is currently no stable accessible online music stream.

nepal.name: Nepal
nepal.intro: The songs of the Himalayan foothills, the ancient rhythms of the Kathmandu Valley.
history: Nepal is the birthplace of the Buddha (Lumbini) and the land of Himalayan peaks (Mount Everest); the temples and palace complexes of the Kathmandu Valley are World Heritage sites.
Its diverse ethnic groups (Newar, Gurung, Sherpa and others) give Nepal an extremely rich folk music tradition.
music: Nepal's music features lok folk songs and instruments such as the madal drum and the sarangi; the Gurung and Sherpa of the mountains and the Newar of the Kathmandu Valley each have their own distinctive song and dance.

musicians.name: Narayan Gopal
musicians.desc: Known as "the Voice of Nepal," he is the most beloved singer in Nepal's modern music history.

radios.name: Radio Nepal
radios.note: Nepal's national broadcaster, playing folk and popular songs.

pakistan.name: Pakistan
pakistan.intro: The shrine of Qawwali and ghazal, the land of Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan.
history: Pakistan gained independence in 1947. Lying at the crossroads of South and Central Asia, it is one of the major countries of the Islamic world; Lahore was once the cultural center of the Mughal Empire.
Pakistan's literary, poetic and musical traditions run deep, and Urdu poetry is the soul of its music.
music: Qawwali is Pakistan's most globally influential music — a Sufi devotional singing that Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan carried across the world. The ghazal poetic-musical tradition and Punjab's bhangra dance music likewise flourish.

musicians.name: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan
musicians.desc: The greatest singer of qawwali music, whose voice shook the world music stage.

musicians.name: Abida Parveen
musicians.desc: Pakistan's most revered Sufi female singer, performing ghazal and qawwali.

radios.name: Radio Pakistan
radios.note: Pakistan's national broadcaster, playing ghazal and classical music.

sri-lanka.name: Sri Lanka
sri-lanka.intro: The pearl of the Indian Ocean, the island rhythms of Kandyan drumming and baila.
history: Sri Lanka, formerly Ceylon, is renowned for its tea, gems and Buddhist holy sites (the Temple of the Tooth in Kandy); its Buddhist tradition dates back more than two thousand years.
The musical traditions of the Sinhalese and Tamil communities together form this island nation's rich soundscape.
music: Sri Lanka's Kandyan drumming and the baila (a lively dance music of Portuguese origin) are the most representative. Sinhalese ritual drumming and Tamil Carnatic music coexist and blend here.

musicians.name: Kandyan Drum Ensemble
musicians.desc: Sri Lankan ritual and festival drumming built around the Kandyan drum.

radios.name: Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation
radios.note: Sri Lanka's national broadcaster, playing baila and Sinhalese music.

united-states.name: United States
united-states.intro: The birthplace of jazz, blues and rock, and a temple of modern classical music and Broadway.
history: The United States was the absolute center of 20th-century popular music: New Orleans gave birth to jazz, the Mississippi Delta to the blues, Memphis and Nashville to rock and country, while New York and Hollywood made musicals and film scores global.
The music of this immigrant nation is the product of the fierce collision of African, European and Latin cultures, giving it unparalleled global reach.
music: Jazz is one of America's greatest original arts: from Louis Armstrong and Duke Ellington to Charlie Parker, Miles Davis and John Coltrane, jazz masters abound. Blues and rock run from Robert Johnson and B.B. King through to Elvis, Bob Dylan and Jimi Hendrix.

In classical music, America produced composers such as Copland, Gershwin, Bernstein, Samuel Barber and Philip Glass, as well as John Williams, the most celebrated contemporary film-score composer; orchestras such as the New York Philharmonic and Chicago Symphony rank among the world's finest, while stations like NPR and WQXR bring classical music to the public.

musicians.name: Louis Armstrong
musicians.desc: A pioneering giant of jazz whose trumpet and gravelly voice defined jazz's golden age.

musicians.name: Duke Ellington
musicians.desc: One of the 20th century's greatest jazz composers, with an astonishing and far-reaching output.

musicians.name: Aaron Copland
musicians.desc: A representative of the "American sound," whose Appalachian Spring and Fanfare for the Common Man are broad and majestic.

musicians.name: George Gershwin
musicians.desc: Blending jazz and classical music, Rhapsody in Blue and An American in Paris are in a class of their own.

musicians.name: Bob Dylan
musicians.desc: A poet of folk and rock, awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016.

radios.name: WQXR (New York)
radios.note: New York's flagship classical station, America's most famous classical music broadcast.

radios.name: NPR Classical / KUSC
radios.note: The classical music program network of American public broadcasting.

radios.name: Jazz24 / WBGO
radios.note: A well-known American jazz station.

radios.name: Great Escape
radios.note: A relaxing channel from Classical California, playing soothing classical music around the clock.

canada.name: Canada
canada.intro: The home of Gould and Oscar Peterson, diverse music across a vast land.
history: Canada is the world's second-largest country by area, with English and French cultures coexisting; the Francophone region of Quebec gives its culture a distinctively European flavor. Its vast nature and Indigenous cultures form the broad, serene foundation of its music.
Though often seen as "the America of the North," Canada has produced countless names who reached the world.
music: In classical music, pianist Glenn Gould became one of the 20th century's most distinctive musicians through his legendary Bach interpretations; in jazz, piano master Oscar Peterson is world-renowned. Singer-songwriters Leonard Cohen, Joni Mitchell and Neil Young, and the diva Céline Dion, make Canada a force in popular music.
The Montreal Symphony Orchestra (long led by Charles Dutoit) and the Toronto Symphony Orchestra are Canada's classical strongholds, while CBC Music links the musical life of the entire country.

musicians.name: Glenn Gould
musicians.desc: Known for his legendary interpretations of Bach's keyboard works, one of the 20th century's most distinctive piano geniuses.

musicians.name: Oscar Peterson
musicians.desc: Canada's greatest jazz musician, with unmatched technique and swing.

musicians.name: Leonard Cohen
musicians.desc: A poetic folk singer-songwriter whose "Hallelujah" has moved generations.

musicians.name: Céline Dion
musicians.desc: An international diva from Quebec, famous for "My Heart Will Go On."

radios.name: CBC Music
radios.note: The music channel of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, playing classical, jazz and indigenous music.

radios.name: ICI Musique
radios.note: The French-language music channel of Canada's broadcaster.

mexico.name: Mexico
mexico.intro: The land of mariachi and ranchera, the symphonic world of Chávez and Revueltas.
history: Mexico is the core of the ancient civilizations of the Americas — Maya and Aztec ruins are found throughout the country, and Spanish colonization after the 16th century left a deep European imprint. Built on the ruins of Tenochtitlan, Mexico City is one of the oldest capitals in the Western Hemisphere.
The Day of the Dead, tequila and the muralist movement (Diego Rivera) together form Mexico's passionate yet profound national character.
music: Mexico's most recognizable sound is the mariachi band — musicians in wide-brimmed sombreros and ornate costumes playing violins, trumpets and guitars while singing ranchera love songs, inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Veracruz's son jarocho and the bolero are equally soulful.

In classical music, Carlos Chávez, Silvestre Revueltas and José Pablo Moncayo (Huapango) fused Mexican folk rhythms into symphonic music, shaping the "Mexican sound"; contemporary tenor Javier Camarena is a star of the world opera stage.

musicians.name: Carlos Chávez
musicians.desc: The founder of modern Mexican music, combining native themes with symphonic language.

musicians.name: Silvestre Revueltas
musicians.desc: One of Mexico's most original composers, whose Sensemayá is vividly colored.

musicians.name: Javier Camarena
musicians.desc: A leading contemporary tenor, known for astonishing high notes in Rossini and Donizetti.

musicians.name: Rolando Villazón
musicians.desc: A Mexico-born world-class tenor and a renowned opera director.

radios.name: Radio UNAM
radios.note: The classical and cultural station of the National Autonomous University of Mexico.

radios.name: Opus 94 (IMER)
radios.note: Mexico's classical music station.

argentina.name: Argentina
argentina.intro: The melancholy capital of tango, the piano empire of Argerich and Barenboim.
history: Argentina is the most Europeanized country in South America; Buenos Aires is called the "Paris of South America," with unforgettable European architecture, steak and café culture. The waves of European immigration at the end of the 19th century shaped its distinctive urban character.
Tango was born in the port neighborhoods of Buenos Aires, rising from working-class dance halls to the world, inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
music: Tango is the soul of Argentina: Carlos Gardel made tango a classic, while Astor Piazzolla's Nuevo Tango brought it into the realm of serious music, with Libertango resounding worldwide.

In classical music, Argentina produced the "high priestess of the piano" Martha Argerich, conductor-pianist Daniel Barenboim, and composer Alberto Ginastera; its classical tradition is second to none in Latin America.

musicians.name: Astor Piazzolla
musicians.desc: The "father of Nuevo Tango," fusing tango with classical and jazz; Libertango is immortal.

musicians.name: Carlos Gardel
musicians.desc: The eternal symbol of tango; "Por una Cabeza" and "El día que me quieras" are still sung today.

musicians.name: Martha Argerich
musicians.desc: One of the greatest living pianists, known for fiery performances and astonishing technique.

musicians.name: Daniel Barenboim
musicians.desc: An Argentine-born musical giant who long led the Berlin State Opera.

radios.name: Radio Nacional Clásica (96.7)
radios.note: Argentina's classical music station.

radios.name: La 2x4 (FM 92.7)
radios.note: Buenos Aires' tango station, playing tango around the clock.

brazil.name: Brazil
brazil.intro: The land of samba and bossa nova, the tropical symphony of Villa-Lobos.
history: Brazil is South America's largest country; Rio de Janeiro's Carnival, Copacabana Beach and the Christ the Redeemer statue are its global icons. As a multi-ethnic melting pot (Portuguese, African and Indigenous), Brazil's music possesses incomparable rhythm and passion.
The Carnival samba parade is the greatest street party on Earth, while football and music are deeply rooted in every Brazilian's blood.
music: Samba is Brazil's soul rhythm, born in Rio's Afro-Brazilian communities; bossa nova made Brazilian music famous worldwide, with "The Girl from Ipanema" becoming a jazz standard. Antônio Carlos Jobim, João Gilberto and Elis Regina define the golden age of MPB (Brazilian popular music).
In classical music, Heitor Villa-Lobos fused Bach with Brazilian folk music, with the Bachianas Brasileiras uniquely charming; Carlos Gomes' opera Il Guarany pioneered the Brazilian opera tradition.

musicians.name: Antônio Carlos Jobim
musicians.desc: The father of bossa nova; "The Girl from Ipanema" and "Desafinado" are immortal.

musicians.name: Heitor Villa-Lobos
musicians.desc: Brazil's greatest composer, whose Bachianas Brasileiras blends Bach with folk music.

musicians.name: João Gilberto
musicians.desc: One of the founders of bossa nova, whose understated singing redefined Brazilian music.

musicians.name: Elis Regina
musicians.desc: The most expressive female singer of the MPB era, hailed as "the voice of Brazil."

radios.name: Rádio Cultura FM
radios.note: São Paulo's classical music station, Brazil's most important classical broadcast.

radios.name: Rádio MEC FM
radios.note: Rio's public classical station.

chile.name: Chile
chile.intro: The land of Nueva Canción and the Araucanía's piano poet, between the Andes and the Pacific.
history: Chile is the world's longest country, stretching between the Andes and the Pacific from the Atacama Desert to the Patagonian ice fields. It has one of South America's most stable institutions, and the poets Neruda and Gabriela Mistral both came from here.
Chilean culture is especially rich in poetry and music; the popular movements deeply shaped its musical expression.
music: Nueva Canción is the pride of Chilean music: Violeta Parra collected folk songs, while Víctor Jara pleaded for the people with his guitar; their voices became the sound of resistance and hope in Latin America. Andean panpipes, the charango and the folk dance cueca are Chile's traditional foundation.
In classical music, piano master Claudio Arrau is one of the 20th century's greatest pianists, with exemplary interpretations of Beethoven and Schumann.

musicians.name: Claudio Arrau
musicians.desc: Chile's greatest musician and one of the pinnacles of 20th-century piano performance.

musicians.name: Violeta Parra
musicians.desc: A pioneer of Nueva Canción; "Gracias a la Vida" is her immortal work.

musicians.name: Víctor Jara
musicians.desc: A symbol of Nueva Canción, whose music and tragic life became a memory of Latin America.

radios.name: Radio Beethoven
radios.note: Santiago's classical music station.

radios.name: Radio Universidad de Chile
radios.note: The cultural station of the University of Chile.

colombia.name: Colombia
colombia.intro: The rhythmic home of cumbia and vallenato, the magical land of García Márquez.
history: Colombia lies in northwestern South America, surrounded by the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific, and is the homeland of literary giant Gabriel García Márquez. Its Andean highlands, Caribbean coast and Amazon rainforest have nurtured an immensely diverse musical culture.
The literary spirit of magical realism also flows through Colombia's passionate and infectious music.
music: Cumbia is Colombia's most representative rhythm, born of African, Indigenous and European fusion and now spread throughout Latin America; vallenato (accordion-led) comes from the life of farmers and herders on the Caribbean coast.
In pop music, Shakira, Carlos Vives and Juanes brought Colombian music worldwide; in classical music, Bogotá's Philharmonic and the Filarmónica Joven youth orchestra system are thriving.

musicians.name: Shakira
musicians.desc: Colombia's most successful international pop star, blending Latin rhythms with global pop.

musicians.name: Carlos Vives
musicians.desc: A Colombian national treasure who combines vallenato with modern pop.

musicians.name: Totó la Momposina
musicians.desc: A guardian of Colombian folk music, known for cumbia and coastal traditions.

radios.name: Señal Clásica
radios.note: Colombia's public classical station.

radios.name: Radiónica
radios.note: Colombia's public broadcaster, playing indigenous and independent music.

peru.name: Peru
peru.intro: The land of Andean panpipes and the African cajón, the homeland of Juan Diego Flórez.
history: Peru is the core of the Inca Empire; the cloud-top ancient city of Machu Picchu is a marvel of human civilization. Andean Quechua culture, coastal Creole culture and Afro-Peruvian traditions meet here.
From the Nazca Lines to colonial Lima, Peru's historical layers are extraordinarily rich.
music: Andean music (zampoña panpipes, the charango and the huayno dance) is the sound of Peru's highlands; the coastal Afro-Peruvian music centers on the cajón (box drum), which singer Susana Baca carried to the world.
In classical music, Peru produced Juan Diego Flórez, one of the finest Rossinian tenors of our time, and Lima's Filarmonía orchestra.

musicians.name: Juan Diego Flórez
musicians.desc: A leading bel canto tenor, known for coloratura and high notes in Rossini.

musicians.name: Susana Baca
musicians.desc: A representative of Afro-Peruvian music, bringing Creole and cajón rhythms to the world.

radios.name: Radio Filarmonía
radios.note: Lima's classical music station.

radios.name: Radio Nacional del Perú
radios.note: Peru's national broadcaster, playing Andean and indigenous music.

venezuela.name: Venezuela
venezuela.intro: The cradle of El Sistema, the land of Dudamel and the harp joropo.
history: Venezuela lies in northern South America; Angel Falls (the world's highest waterfall) and the vast llanos plains are its natural icons. Oil once made it prosperous, and also brought upheaval.
Despite the country's turmoil, Venezuela possesses Latin America's proudest musical education miracle.
music: What most astonished the world about Venezuela is not a single star but a system — El Sistema, which used classical music education to change the fate of hundreds of thousands of poor children, and produced conductor Gustavo Dudamel. Its folk music includes the joropo (a lively harp-led dance) of the llanos plains.

musicians.name: Gustavo Dudamel
musicians.desc: A world-class conductor trained by El Sistema, long-time leader of the Los Angeles Philharmonic.

musicians.name: Teresa Carreño
musicians.desc: A legendary 19th-century pianist and composer; Caracas' national theater is named after her.

radios.name: Radio Clásica Venezuela
radios.note: Venezuela's classical music station.

uruguay.name: Uruguay
uruguay.intro: The candombe drums and tango on the shores of the Río de la Plata, South America's small and beautiful country.
history: Uruguay lies between the Río de la Plata and the Atlantic, one of South America's most tranquil and progressive small nations. Montevideo's old town and waterfront promenade are full of the leisurely Río de la Plata charm.
It shares the Río de la Plata tango culture with Argentina, while also possessing its own distinctive Afro-Uruguayan musical tradition.
music: Candombe is Uruguay's national treasure — a drumming parade rooted in Afro-descendant communities, now inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity; during Carnival the whole city of Montevideo moves to its rhythm. Singers Alfredo Zitarrosa and Jaime Roos recorded Uruguayans' nostalgia and humor in song.

musicians.name: Alfredo Zitarrosa
musicians.desc: Uruguay's most beloved folk singer, whose deep, soulful voice touched people's hearts.

musicians.name: Jaime Roos
musicians.desc: A Uruguayan music master who blends candombe, tango and rock.

radios.name: Radio Clásica SODRE
radios.note: Uruguay's public classical station.

ecuador.name: Ecuador
ecuador.intro: The land of the Equator, the heartfelt home of Andean sanjuanito and pasillo.
history: Ecuador is named for the Equator that crosses it; the old town of its capital Quito was the first UNESCO World Heritage city. The unique ecology of the Galápagos Islands makes it a mecca for nature lovers.
Its Andean highlands, coast and Amazon regions shape a diverse musical landscape.
music: Ecuador's music is represented by the Andean sanjuanito (a lively festive dance) and the pasillo (a wistful waltz-like love song), with the charango, panpipes and guitar weaving moving melodies.

musicians.name: Julio Jaramillo
musicians.desc: The "voice of Ecuador," who made the pasillo a shared memory across Latin America.

radios.name: Radio Pública del Ecuador
radios.note: Ecuador's public broadcaster, playing indigenous music.

bolivia.name: Bolivia
bolivia.intro: The highland country of the charango and sikuri panpipes, the musical heart of the Andes.
history: Bolivia is known for La Paz, the world's highest capital, and Lake Titicaca, and is one of the South American countries where Indigenous culture is best preserved. Aymara and Quechua traditions remain alive here.
The "Mirror of the Sky" Salar de Uyuni and the grandeur of the Andean plateau shape its powerful, far-reaching musical character.
music: Bolivia is a stronghold of Andean music: the sikuri panpipe ensembles, the charango (a small plucked instrument traditionally made from an armadillo shell) and the caporales dance are all cultural treasures. The saya drumming of Afro-Bolivian communities is equally distinctive.

musicians.name: Los Kjarkas
musicians.desc: Bolivia's most famous Andean music group; their hit "Llorando se fue" was adapted into the worldwide hit "Lambada."

radios.name: Radio Nacional de Bolivia
radios.note: Bolivia's national broadcaster, playing Andean music.

paraguay.name: Paraguay
paraguay.intro: The land of the Paraguayan harp and guarania, the guitar poetry of Barrios.
history: Paraguay is a landlocked South American country, unique in that Guaraní — an Indigenous language — shares official status with Spanish, something unprecedented in the Americas. Asunción and the Jesuit mission ruins testify to its colonial history.
This bilingual, mixed culture fills Paraguayan music with a unique tenderness and nostalgia.
music: Paraguay is famous for the harp: the arpeggios of the Paraguayan harp (arpa paraguaya) flow like water, while the guarania and the polka paraguaya are its signature dances. Guitar master Agustín Barrios (Mangoré) is one of Latin America's greatest classical guitar composers.

musicians.name: Agustín Barrios (Mangoré)
musicians.desc: Latin America's greatest classical guitar composer; La Catedral and the last tremolo are deeply moving.

musicians.name: José Asunción Flores
musicians.desc: The creator of the guarania genre, whose music became the soul of Paraguay.

radios.name: Radio Nacional del Paraguay
radios.note: Paraguay's national broadcaster, playing harp and guarania music.

belize.name: Belize
belize.intro: The English-speaking small nation of the Caribbean coast, a world heritage of Garifuna drumming.
history: Belize is Central America's only English-speaking country (formerly British Honduras), on the Caribbean coast with the world's second-largest barrier reef.
Maya civilization, Afro-descendant Garifuna and Creole cultures meet here, shaping its distinctive musical landscape.
music: Belize's Garifuna music (including drumming, song and dance) is inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, originating with the Afro-descendant Garifuna of St. Vincent in the Caribbean. Brukdown is the Creole dance music.

musicians.name: Andy Palacio
musicians.desc: A promoter of Belizean Garifuna music, whose album Wátina won international acclaim.

belize.radioNote: Belize's broadcasting is mainly in English and Creole; there is currently no stable accessible online music stream.

costa-rica.name: Costa Rica
costa-rica.intro: The land of "Pura Vida," the leisurely rhythms of marimba and calypso.
history: Costa Rica is known for the life philosophy of "Pura Vida" (pure life); it is the most stable and highly educated country in Central America, and one of the few nations in the world without an army.
Rainforests, volcanoes and beaches form its leisurely and abundant natural backdrop.
music: Costa Rica's traditional music features the marimba (xylophone) ensemble and the calypso of the Caribbean coast, with folk dances such as the tambito and the punto widely popular.

musicians.name: Orquesta Sinfónica Nacional
musicians.desc: Costa Rica's national symphony orchestra, a stronghold of classical music in Central America.

radios.name: Radio Universidad de Costa Rica
radios.note: The cultural station of the University of Costa Rica.

el-salvador.name: El Salvador
el-salvador.intro: The land of volcanoes in Central America, the home of cumbia and Pipil traditions.
history: El Salvador is Central America's smallest country by area, known for its many volcanoes and coffee. Indigenous Pipil traditions and Spanish colonial culture blend here.
Despite its small size, El Salvador's folk music and festival culture are extraordinarily vibrant.
music: El Salvador's traditional music blends Indigenous Pipil elements with Spanish and African rhythms, represented by the chanchona (a rural band featuring the bass drum) and cumbia.

musicians.name: Chanchona Ensemble
musicians.desc: A classic band form of Salvadoran rural festivals, featuring bass drums and strings.

el-salvador.radioNote: El Salvador's broadcasting is mainly pop and general programming; there is currently no stable accessible online music stream.

guatemala.name: Guatemala
guatemala.intro: The heart of Maya civilization, the homeland of the marimba.
history: Guatemala is one of the centers of ancient Maya civilization, with the pyramid temples of Tikal rising majestically from the jungle. It is Central America's most populous country with the strongest Indigenous culture.
Maya descendants still preserve a rich array of traditional dress, languages and ritual music.
music: Guatemala is known as "the homeland of the marimba"; this large xylophone has been declared its national treasure instrument, and marimba ensembles run through festivals and daily life. Maya traditional music and Spanish colonial music blend here.

musicians.name: Marimba Chapinlandia
musicians.desc: One of Guatemala's most famous marimba ensembles, spreading the sound of the marimba worldwide.

radios.name: Radio Nacional TGW
radios.note: Guatemala's national broadcaster, playing marimba and folk music.

honduras.name: Honduras
honduras.intro: The land of the Copán Maya ruins and punta dance music.
history: Honduras lies in northern Central America; the Maya ruins of Copán are an important testament to ancient Maya civilization. Afro-descendant Garifuna on the Caribbean coast and inland mestizo culture together form its diverse society.
music: Honduras' music is best known for the punta (the fast-paced dance music of the Garifuna) of the Caribbean coast, whose fiery drumbeats are infectious and have become an iconic Central American rhythm.

musicians.name: Aurelio Martínez
musicians.desc: A representative of Honduran Garifuna music, bringing punta and Garifuna tradition to the world.

honduras.radioNote: Honduras' broadcasting is mainly pop and general programming; there is currently no stable accessible online music stream.

nicaragua.name: Nicaragua
nicaragua.intro: The land of lakes and volcanoes, the home of Palo de Mayo and the marimba.
history: Nicaragua is known for Lake Nicaragua and its many volcanoes, and was the stage of Spanish colonization and the Sandinista revolution. The poet Rubén Darío is the founder of Spanish-language modernist literature.
music: Nicaragua's traditional music features the marimba and the Palo de Mayo (Maypole song and dance of the Caribbean coast), the latter rooted in Afro-descendant carnival traditions.

musicians.name: Carlos Mejía Godoy
musicians.desc: Nicaragua's most representative singer-songwriter, whose songs recorded the nation's revolution and hope.

nicaragua.radioNote: Nicaragua's broadcasting is mainly general programming; there is currently no stable accessible online music stream.

panama.name: Panama
panama.intro: The hub of the Panama Canal, the passion of tamborito and salsa.
history: Panama is known for the Panama Canal linking the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, and is Central America's economic hub. Its diverse immigrants (Afro-descendant, Caribbean, Chinese and others) shape an open and multicultural society.
music: Panama's traditional music features the tamborito (a song-and-dance featuring drums and chorus) and the mejorana; in pop music, singer Rubén Blades made Panamanian salsa world-famous.

musicians.name: Rubén Blades
musicians.desc: A legendary figure of salsa music, as well as a Harvard-educated lawyer and politician.

radios.name: Radio Nacional de Panamá
radios.note: Panama's national broadcaster, playing salsa and indigenous music.

cuba.name: Cuba
cuba.intro: The melodic heart of Havana, the land of son, rumba and the Buena Vista Social Club.
history: Cuba is the largest island nation in the Caribbean; Havana's old town and vintage cars, Hemingway's former home and cigars form its unique charm. After the 1959 revolution, it took a distinctive socialist path.
