African, Spanish and Caribbean musical traditions are fused here into a deeply infectious Cuban sound.
music: Cuban music has influenced the world profoundly: son, rumba, cha-cha-chá, mambo and the veteran musicians of the Buena Vista Social Club spread Cuban rhythms worldwide. In classical music, Cuba has the most complete music education system in the Caribbean, producing many first-rate musicians.

musicians.name: Benny Moré
musicians.desc: Hailed as the "King of Cuban Music," his voice and charisma were unmatched.

musicians.name: Celia Cruz
musicians.desc: The "Queen of Salsa," a global symbol of Cuban music.

musicians.name: Leo Brouwer
musicians.desc: One of Cuba's greatest classical guitar composers.

radios.name: Radio Musical Nacional
radios.note: Cuba's national music station.

dominican-republic.name: Dominican Republic
dominican-republic.intro: The home of merengue and bachata, the passionate rhythms of Santo Domingo.
history: The Dominican Republic shares the island of Hispaniola with Haiti; its capital, Santo Domingo, is the earliest European city established in the Americas. Its colonial history and Afro-descendant culture are deeply intertwined.
Music is the core of Dominican life, its rhythms full of Caribbean sunshine and passion.
music: The Dominican Republic contributed two globally popular rhythms: merengue (a fast, lively two-beat dance) and bachata (a soulful guitar love song), both inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

musicians.name: Juan Luis Guerra
musicians.desc: The Dominican Republic's most famous musician, bringing merengue and bachata to the world.

radios.name: Radio Clásica / Quisqueya FM
radios.note: The Dominican Republic's classical and pop stations.

haiti.name: Haiti
haiti.intro: The land of Vodou drumming and kompa, the cradle of Caribbean freedom.
history: Haiti is the first Black republic in the Americas, winning independence through a slave revolt in 1804; its spirit of freedom shook the world.
African Vodou beliefs and French colonial culture intertwine here, giving birth to a distinctive Haitian music.
music: Haiti's music is best known for Vodou ritual drumming and the kompa (a lively dance music derived from merengue), fiery in rhythm and rich in ritual feeling. Rara parade music fills the streets during Easter.

musicians.name: Tabou Combo
musicians.desc: Haiti's most internationally influential kompa band, bringing Haitian rhythms to the world.

haiti.radioNote: Due to economic and infrastructure conditions, Haiti currently has no stable accessible online music stream.

jamaica.name: Jamaica
jamaica.intro: The home of reggae and Bob Marley, the musical mecca of the Caribbean.
history: Jamaica is the third-largest island in the Caribbean; Kingston's music scene gave birth to a pop music revolution that influenced the whole world. This sparsely populated island's musical influence far exceeds its size.
music: Jamaica contributed ska, rocksteady, reggae and dancehall — a series of world-changing musical forms. Bob Marley brought reggae and the Rastafari faith to the world, becoming one of the greatest music icons of the 20th century.

musicians.name: Bob Marley
musicians.desc: The global symbol of reggae, whose music and spirit were profoundly influential.

musicians.name: Jimmy Cliff
musicians.desc: One of the pioneers of reggae, known for "The Harder They Come."

radios.name: Irie FM / KOOL 97
radios.note: Jamaica's reggae music station.

trinidad-and-tobago.name: Trinidad and Tobago
trinidad-and-tobago.intro: The birthplace of steelpan and calypso, the rhythmic heart of Carnival.
history: Trinidad and Tobago is the southernmost island nation in the Caribbean; its Carnival is the largest celebration in the region. The blending of Indian and African cultures makes its music exceptionally rich.
music: Trinidad contributed two unique musical forms: the steelpan (a melodic percussion instrument made from discarded oil drums, the only acoustic instrument newly invented in the 20th century) and calypso (witty narrative song), as well as soca dance music.

musicians.name: Steelpan Orchestra
musicians.desc: The ensemble of Trinidad's national treasure, the steelpan, with bell-like tones and majestic power.

trinidad-and-tobago.radioNote: Trinidad and Tobago's broadcasting focuses on soca and calypso; there is currently no stable accessible online music stream.

bahamas.name: Bahamas
bahamas.intro: An archipelago of seven hundred islands, with junkyard steel drums and Junkanoo carnival.
history: The Bahamas is made up of more than seven hundred islands, once a stronghold of pirates and maritime trade, and today famous for its pink-sand beaches and turquoise waters.
music: Bahamian music is best known for the cowbells, drums and whistles of Junkanoo (the festival parade), while "rake-and-scrape" (played with a saw blade and accordion) is its distinctive folk genre.

musicians.name: Junkanoo Band
musicians.desc: The drum-and-horn band of the Bahamian festival parade, with hot, infectious rhythms.

bahamas.radioNote: Broadcasting in the Bahamas focuses on tourism and general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

barbados.name: Barbados
barbados.intro: The home of Rihanna, an island nation of calypso and spouge music.
history: Barbados is the easternmost island nation in the Caribbean, a former British colony that grew from sugarcane cultivation and sugar refining, and is today one of the most developed countries in the Caribbean.
music: Barbadian music features calypso and "spouge," a rhythm blending ska and soul. Global pop superstar Rihanna took the world stage from here.

musicians.name: Rihanna
musicians.desc: A global pop icon from Barbados who has repeatedly topped international charts.

barbados.radioNote: Broadcasting in Barbados focuses on pop and calypso; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

saint-lucia.name: Saint Lucia
saint-lucia.intro: A volcanic island nation beneath the Pitons, with kadans and Kwéyòl music.
history: Saint Lucia is famous for the twin peaks of the Pitons and is one of the most beautiful volcanic islands in the Caribbean. Alternating British and French colonial rule left behind its distinctive Kwéyòl culture.
music: Saint Lucia hosts the Caribbean's only jazz and arts festival; its traditional kadans, Kwéyòl folk music, and the drum-dance "kwadril" are all distinctive.

musicians.name: St. Lucia Jazz Ensemble
musicians.desc: A representative ensemble of the Saint Lucia Jazz Festival, blending Caribbean rhythms with jazz.

saint-lucia.radioNote: Broadcasting in Saint Lucia focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

saint-vincent-and-the-grenadines.name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
saint-vincent-and-the-grenadines.intro: An island nation of volcanoes and islets, the source of big drum music and the Garifuna.
history: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines is made up of the main island of Saint Vincent and a chain of Grenadine islets, and is one of the birthplaces of Garifuna culture.
music: Saint Vincent is an important custodian of "big drum," the ceremonial drum music of the Garifuna people, a drumming tradition shared with the Garifuna music of Belize and Honduras.

musicians.name: Big Drum Ensemble
musicians.desc: The ceremonial drum music of the Garifuna people of Saint Vincent, solemn and powerful in rhythm.

saint-vincent-and-the-grenadines.radioNote: Broadcasting in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

grenada.name: Grenada
grenada.intro: Calypso and steelpan on the "Isle of Spice," a small Caribbean gem.
history: Grenada is known for spices such as nutmeg and is called the "Isle of Spice." Its volcanoes, waterfalls and turquoise seas form a quintessential Caribbean landscape.
music: Grenadian music centers on calypso and steelpan, and the calypso competition during carnival is a major cultural event across the island.

musicians.name: Grenada Steelband
musicians.desc: A steelpan ensemble of the Grenada carnival, bright and cheerful in tone.

grenada.radioNote: Broadcasting in Grenada focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

dominica.name: Dominica
dominica.intro: Garifuna and Kwéyòl music of the "Nature Isle."
history: Dominica (not to be confused with the Dominican Republic) is known as the "Nature Isle," home to the Caribbean's best-preserved tropical rainforest and volcanic hot springs.
music: Dominican music features Kwéyòl folk songs, kadans and "bouyon," a dance music that fuses several Caribbean rhythms.

musicians.name: WCK Band
musicians.desc: The most representative bouyon band of Dominica, with hot, driving rhythms.

dominica.radioNote: Broadcasting in Dominica focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

antigua-and-barbuda.name: Antigua and Barbuda
antigua-and-barbuda.intro: The island nation of "365 beaches," with steelpan and calypso festivities.
history: Antigua and Barbuda is made up of Antigua, Barbuda and other islands, and is said to have 365 beaches (one for each day of the year). A former British colony, it now relies on tourism as its mainstay.
music: Antiguan music centers on calypso, steelpan and carnival music; its carnival is one of the oldest in the Caribbean.

musicians.name: Antigua Steelband
musicians.desc: A steelpan ensemble of the Antigua carnival, rich in festive atmosphere.

antigua-and-barbuda.radioNote: Broadcasting in Antigua and Barbuda focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

saint-kitts-and-nevis.name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
saint-kitts-and-nevis.intro: Calypso and steelpan of the twin-island nation, the sugarcane homeland of the Caribbean.
history: Saint Kitts and Nevis is made up of the two islands of Saint Kitts and Nevis, among the first British Caribbean islands to be colonized, and once known for sugarcane cultivation.
music: The music of Saint Kitts and Nevis features calypso, steelpan, and the street drumming of the carnival known as "J'ouvert."

musicians.name: St. Kitts Steelband
musicians.desc: A steelpan ensemble of the Saint Kitts carnival, rich in festive atmosphere.

saint-kitts-and-nevis.radioNote: Broadcasting in Saint Kitts and Nevis focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

guyana.name: Guyana
guyana.intro: South America's only English-speaking country, a rainforest land of chutney and Caribbean rhythms.
history: Guyana lies in northeastern South America and is the only country on the continent with English as its official language. Indian, African and indigenous cultures intermingle deeply here.
Its vast tropical rainforest and Kaieteur Falls (among the world's highest single-drop waterfalls) are its natural wonders.
music: Guyanese music blends Caribbean and Indian elements: "chutney" (a dance music of the Indian community fusing calypso with Indian music), calypso and soca are all widely popular.

musicians.name: Eddy Grant
musicians.desc: A musician of Guyanese descent, whose "Electric Avenue" is a global pop classic.

guyana.radioNote: Broadcasting in Guyana focuses on pop and general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

suriname.name: Suriname
suriname.intro: The smallest country in South America, a rich blend of kaseko and Javanese gamelan.
history: Suriname is the smallest country in South America, formerly Dutch Guiana. Its diverse communities—African, Indian, Javanese, Chinese and indigenous—make it one of the most culturally distinctive countries on the continent.
music: Surinamese music is the product of its diverse communities: "kaseko" (a percussion dance music of the African community), Javanese gamelan, and the Indian community's baithak gana coexist here, forming a rare musical kaleidoscope.

musicians.name: Kaseko Ensemble
musicians.desc: The percussion dance music of Suriname's African community, hot, rhythmic and full of vitality.

suriname.radioNote: Broadcasting in Suriname is mainly in Dutch and local languages; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

australia.name: Australia
australia.intro: The ancient drone of the didgeridoo and the operatic miracle of Joan Sutherland.
history: Australia is one of the oldest continents on Earth, with an Indigenous culture stretching back at least sixty thousand years; the drone of the didgeridoo is the oldest sound of this land. After British colonization in the 18th century, it developed into a diverse immigrant nation.
The sail-like form of the Sydney Opera House is one of the greatest buildings of the 20th century and made Australia an important center of classical music in the Southern Hemisphere.
music: In classical music, Australia gave the world one of the greatest coloratura sopranos of the 20th century, Joan Sutherland, as well as composer Percy Grainger; the Sydney Symphony Orchestra and Melbourne Symphony Orchestra are pillars of the Southern Hemisphere's music scene, while ABC Classic brings classical music into homes across the country.
In pop, names such as AC/DC, INXS and Kylie Minogue made Australia a major source of rock and pop.

musicians.name: Dame Joan Sutherland
musicians.desc: "The Voice of the Century," one of the greatest coloratura sopranos of the 20th century, hailed as "La Stupenda."

musicians.name: Percy Grainger
musicians.desc: An Australian composer known for works such as "Country Gardens," devoted to collecting folk music.

musicians.name: AC/DC
musicians.desc: Australia's most successful rock band; "Back in Black" is one of the best-selling albums in history.

radios.name: ABC Classic
radios.note: The classical channel of the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, the most important classical station in the Southern Hemisphere.

radios.name: Double J
radios.note: The music channel of the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, focused on independent music.

new-zealand.name: New Zealand
new-zealand.intro: The home of the Māori haka and Kiri Te Kanawa, the pure sound of the Southern Hemisphere.
history: New Zealand (Aotearoa in Māori, meaning "the land of the long white cloud") is made up of the North and South Islands and is known for its magnificent fjords, volcanoes and Māori culture. The Māori "haka" war dance has become a cultural symbol of the country.
The Lord of the Rings trilogy was filmed here, revealing its Middle-earth-like fantasy landscapes to the world.
music: Māori music in New Zealand features the haka, poi song-and-dance and the nose flute (koauau), full of power and ritual. In classical music, soprano Kiri Te Kanawa is a legend of the world's opera stages, while the New Zealand Symphony Orchestra gives the island nation a first-rate classical force in the Southern Hemisphere.
In pop, Lorde became the brightest contemporary New Zealand voice with "Royals."

musicians.name: Dame Kiri Te Kanawa
musicians.desc: A world-class soprano of Māori descent, celebrated worldwide for her interpretations of Mozart and Strauss.

musicians.name: Lorde
musicians.desc: A representative of New Zealand's new generation of singer-songwriters; "Royals" won a Grammy Award.

radios.name: RNZ Concert
radios.note: The classical channel of Radio New Zealand.

radios.name: RNZ National
radios.note: The national channel of Radio New Zealand, also broadcasting Māori music.

fiji.name: Fiji
fiji.intro: A pearl of the South Pacific, where meke song-and-dance meets Indian chutney.
history: Fiji is an island nation in the South Pacific made up of more than three hundred islands, known for its coral reefs and turquoise seas. Its society is formed by two major communities, the Indian and the indigenous Fijian.
music: Traditional Fijian music centers on "meke," a performance combining song, dance and chant, often accompanied by drums, hand-clapping and seated dances. The Indian community brought chutney and baithak gana music, creating a distinctive cultural fusion.

musicians.name: Meke Ensemble
musicians.desc: A traditional Fijian performance that recounts legends and history through song, dance and chant.

fiji.radioNote: Broadcasting in Fiji focuses on general and tourism programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

papua-new-guinea.name: Papua New Guinea
papua-new-guinea.intro: A cultural kaleidoscope of eight hundred languages, with bamboo bands and garamut drums of the jungle.
history: Papua New Guinea has more than eight hundred languages and is one of the most linguistically and culturally diverse countries in the world. Tribal traditions in its highland valleys and jungles remain vividly alive today.
music: The music of Papua New Guinea is extraordinarily diverse: tribal song-and-dance of the highlands and jungles, the "garamut" (a drum made from a hollowed tree trunk) and the "bamboo band" (played by striking bamboo tubes) are all distinctive.

musicians.name: Garamut Drum Ensemble
musicians.desc: Ritual music of Papua New Guinea played on large wooden drums made from hollowed tree trunks.

papua-new-guinea.radioNote: Broadcasting in Papua New Guinea focuses on tribal languages and general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

solomon-islands.name: Solomon Islands
solomon-islands.intro: A Melanesian archipelago, with panpipe ensembles and the tradition of war chants.
history: The Solomon Islands is made up of nearly a thousand islands and was a major theater of the Pacific War in World War II. Melanesian tribal culture remains vigorous here.
music: The Solomon Islands is famous for its panpipe ensembles; bamboo panpipes of different lengths play airy, richly layered music, one of Melanesia's most distinctive musical traditions.

musicians.name: Solomon Islands Panpipe Ensemble
musicians.desc: Traditional Melanesian music played on bamboo panpipes, airy and ethereal in tone.

solomon-islands.radioNote: Broadcasting in the Solomon Islands focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

vanuatu.name: Vanuatu
vanuatu.intro: An island nation of water music and string instruments, a living Melanesian tradition.
history: Vanuatu is made up of more than eighty volcanic islands, known for its active volcanoes and distinctive tribal culture. Bislama, an English-based creole, is the lingua franca.
music: Vanuatu has one of the world's most distinctive musical traditions: "water music," in which women slap the surface of shallow water to create rhythm, is inscribed on UNESCO's list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity. In addition, the string instrument "aumu" and tribal ritual song-and-dance are rich and varied.

musicians.name: Water Music Ensemble
musicians.desc: A unique performance in which Vanuatu women slap the water's surface to create rhythm, inscribed on the list of humanity's intangible cultural heritage.

vanuatu.radioNote: Broadcasting in Vanuatu focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

micronesia.name: Federated States of Micronesia
micronesia.intro: An island nation of the western Pacific, an ocean civilization of canoes and navigation chants.
history: The Federated States of Micronesia is made up of more than six hundred islands; its ancestors were renowned for masterful canoe navigation and celestial wayfinding, and their crossings of the Pacific are astonishing.
music: The music of Micronesia is inseparable from the sea and navigation; navigation chants, canoe paddling songs and the stick dance are its traditional performance forms.

musicians.name: Micronesian Canoe Chant
musicians.desc: Micronesian chants tied to seafaring traditions, with rhythms synchronized to paddling.

micronesia.radioNote: Broadcasting in the Federated States of Micronesia focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

kiribati.name: Kiribati
kiribati.intro: An island nation straddling the Equator and the Date Line, with solo dance and hand-drum rhythms of the ocean.
history: Kiribati is made up of thirty-three atolls spanning the Equator and the International Date Line, one of the most dispersed countries in the world. Rising sea levels are threatening this low-lying land.
music: Kiribati music features the solo dance (ruoia), stick dance and choral singing, with hand-drums and hand-clapping rhythms running through its festivals and rituals. Its "te kaini kamana" singing tradition is passed down through the generations.

musicians.name: Kiribati Dance Ensemble
musicians.desc: A traditional Kiribati performance centered on the stick dance and hand-drum, with lively rhythms.

kiribati.radioNote: Broadcasting in Kiribati focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

marshall-islands.name: Marshall Islands
marshall-islands.intro: A seafaring civilization on a chain of atolls, with stick charts and choral ocean traditions.
history: The Marshall Islands is made up of more than a thousand islands and atolls; the stick charts invented by its ancestors used sticks and shells to record ocean currents and island positions, a unique seafaring wisdom.
music: Traditional Marshallese music features choral singing and the stick dance; its distinctive "aolep" chanting and navigation songs record the islanders' intimate relationship with the sea.

musicians.name: Marshallese Choir
musicians.desc: A group performing traditional Marshallese songs in multi-part harmony.

marshall-islands.radioNote: Broadcasting in the Marshall Islands focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

nauru.name: Nauru
nauru.intro: One of the world's smallest island nations, the songs of a phosphate island.
history: Nauru is the third smallest country in the world by area (after Monaco and Vatican City) and was once wealthy thanks to its phosphate deposits. This isolated coral island has its own distinctive language and culture.
music: Nauruan traditional music accompanies choral singing and dance; its distinctive "te ilo" singing tradition and the stick dance are performed at festivals, deeply influenced by Micronesian culture.

musicians.name: Nauruan Dance Ensemble
musicians.desc: Traditional song-and-dance performances at Nauruan festivals, with lively rhythms.

nauru.radioNote: Broadcasting in Nauru focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

palau.name: Palau
palau.intro: A diving paradise of the Rock Islands, with women's stick dances and traditional songs.
history: Palau is known for the mushroom-shaped limestone islands of the Rock Islands and its superb diving environment, a global model of marine conservation.
music: Palauan traditional music features women's stick dances and choral singing; its distinctive "chesbich" chants record tribal history and legend.

musicians.name: Palauan Stick Dance Ensemble
musicians.desc: A performing group presenting Palauan tradition through stick dance and choral singing.

palau.radioNote: Broadcasting in Palau focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

samoa.name: Samoa
samoa.intro: The heart of Polynesia, with siva dance and pātē drum music.
history: Samoa is one of the cores of Polynesian culture and is regarded as the "cradle" of Polynesia. Its traditional "Fa'a Samoa" (the Samoan way) has deeply influenced the entire Pacific island region.
music: Samoan music features choral singing and the "siva" dance; the "pātē" (log drum), hand-clapping and seated rhythms blend in perfect accord. Samoans' choral talent is especially outstanding among Pacific islanders.

musicians.name: Samoan Choir
musicians.desc: Multi-part Samoan choral singing, powerful and harmonious in sound.

samoa.radioNote: Broadcasting in Samoa focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

tonga.name: Tonga
tonga.intro: The last kingdom of the Pacific, with the rhythms of lakalaka and the tufakana drum.
history: Tonga is the only remaining monarchy in the Pacific, its royal line spanning a thousand years. As an important center of Polynesia, Tonga has deep traditions.
music: Tongan music is best known for the "lakalaka," a collective song-and-dance inscribed on UNESCO's list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity; the synchronized song-and-dance of hundreds of people, driven by the "tufakana" drum, is majestic.

musicians.name: Lakalaka Ensemble
musicians.desc: A collective Tongan song-and-dance on a scale of hundreds, inscribed on the list of humanity's intangible cultural heritage.

tonga.radioNote: Broadcasting in Tonga focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

tuvalu.name: Tuvalu
tuvalu.intro: The "nation of eight islands" on low-lying atolls, with fatele song-and-dance and the worry of rising seas.
history: Tuvalu is made up of nine low-lying atolls, one of the world's smallest countries and among the most threatened by rising sea levels. Its traditional "fatele" song-and-dance carries the islanders' historical memory.
music: Tuvalu's "fatele" is a traditional performance centered on choral singing and dance, its rhythms played on wooden boxes and hand-claps, often recounting stories of seafaring and family.

musicians.name: Fatele Ensemble
musicians.desc: A performance presenting Tuvaluan tradition through choral singing, dance and box-drum rhythms.

tuvalu.radioNote: Broadcasting in Tuvalu focuses on general programming; there is currently no stable, accessible online music stream.

morocco.name: Morocco
morocco.intro: Gnawa and Andalusi classical music of the Maghreb, a soundscape between the Atlas Mountains and the Sahara.
history: Morocco is the westernmost kingdom of the Maghreb, having passed through Arab dynasties, the Berber empires and the French protectorate, and is today one of the most culturally dynamic countries in northwestern Africa. The famous cities of Marrakesh, Fez and Casablanca bear witness to the meeting of Arab, Berber and Andalusi civilizations.
music: The hallmark of Moroccan music is Gnawa—a trance-inducing sound fusing African rhythms, Sufi ritual and Berber tradition, inscribed on UNESCO's list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity; the Andalusi classical music (al-âla) originating in medieval Iberia is also preserved here to this day. The Berber Amazigh music of the Atlas Mountains excels in drums and throat-singing-like chanting.

musicians.name: Nass El Ghiwane
musicians.desc: Called the "Rolling Stones of Morocco," bringing Gnawa and folk music into a modern context.

musicians.name: Laila Lalami
musicians.desc: A Moroccan-born writer whose words carry the sonic memory of the Maghreb.

radios.name: Radio 2M / Médi 1
radios.note: A mainstream Moroccan station playing local and Arab pop music.

algeria.name: Algeria
algeria.intro: The birthplace of Raï, where Cheb Khaled carried the sound of North Africa to the world.
history: Algeria is the largest country in Africa by area, having passed through the Berber kingdoms, the Ottoman province and more than 130 years of French colonization; the trauma and pride of the war of independence profoundly shaped its culture.
music: Algeria contributed North Africa's most globally influential music—Raï, an urban pop born in the port of Oran that fuses Berber folk with Bedouin melodies, made world-famous by Cheb Khaled, Cheb Mami and others. In addition, the Berber music of the Kabylie mountains and Andalusi classical music have deep roots here.

musicians.name: Cheb Khaled
musicians.desc: The "King of Raï," who brought Algerian pop to the world with "Aïcha" and "Didi."

musicians.name: Rachid Taha
musicians.desc: A pioneer who fused Raï with rock and electronic music.

radios.name: Radio Algérie Chaine 3
radios.note: The national broadcaster of Algeria, playing Raï and traditional music.

tunisia.name: Tunisia
tunisia.intro: The poetic home of Malouf Andalusi classical music and the oud.
history: Tunisia is the land of ancient Carthage, having passed through Roman, Arab, Ottoman and French protectorate rule, and is one of the most secular and culturally refined countries of the Maghreb; the Roman amphitheater of El Jem and the blue-and-white town of Sidi Bou Said are its calling cards.
music: Tunisia's signature is "malouf," a classical vocal tradition of Andalusi origin inscribed on UNESCO's list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity; in addition, oud playing and Tunisia's own stambeli (a ritual music of sub-Saharan origin) are equally captivating.

musicians.name: Anouar Brahem
musicians.desc: A world-class oud player, known for ECM recordings that fuse jazz and Arab classical music.

radios.name: Radio Tunis Chaîne Internationale
radios.note: The international channel of the national broadcaster of Tunisia.

libya.name: Libya
libya.intro: The makam tradition and Saharan Bedouin melodies, a vast soundscape on the southern shore of the Mediterranean.
history: Libya spans the southern shore of the Mediterranean; in antiquity it was part of Carthaginian and Roman territory, and the ruins of Leptis Magna remain spectacular to this day. In modern times it has endured Italian colonization and prolonged turmoil, but its folk music traditions have remained resilient.
music: Libyan music is built on the Arabic "makam" system, blending Bedouin nomadic melodies with Mediterranean flavor; at traditional weddings and festivals, the oud, drums and unison choral singing take center stage, and the malouf tradition of Tripoli shares a lineage with those of Tunisia and Algeria.

musicians.name: Libyan Folk Ensemble
musicians.desc: A Libyan folk music group carrying on the Bedouin and makam traditions.

radios.name: Libya Radio
radios.note: The national broadcaster of Libya.

egypt.name: Egypt
egypt.intro: The musical center of the Arab world, the golden voice of Umm Kulthum and the cradle of Cairo's classical music.
history: Egypt is an ancient civilization on the banks of the Nile; the pyramids, the Karnak temple complex and historic Cairo bear witness to seven thousand years of splendor. In the 20th century, Cairo became the cultural capital of the entire Arab world, its cinema, music and broadcasting influencing the Middle East and North Africa.
music: Egypt is a major center of Arab classical music: Umm Kulthum, hailed as the "Star of the East," held the entire Arab world breathless with her epic singing; masters such as Mohammed Abdel Wahab and Abdel Halim Hafez together forged Cairo's golden age. The orchestral tradition of the Cairo Arabic Music Institute remains among the most authoritative in Arab music today.

musicians.name: Umm Kulthum
musicians.desc: The "Star of the East," the most influential singer of the 20th-century Arab world.

musicians.name: Abdel Halim Hafez
musicians.desc: A legendary Egyptian singer and actor whose heartfelt voice is still sung today.

musicians.name: Mohammed Abdel Wahab
musicians.desc: A pioneer who introduced Western instruments into Arab classical music.

radios.name: Nile FM / Radio Masr
radios.note: A mainstream music station in Cairo.

sudan.name: Sudan
sudan.intro: The thousand-year echo of Nubian music and makam, a soundscape at the confluence of the Nile.
history: Sudan lies at the confluence of the two main branches of the Nile and was the heartland of the ancient Kingdom of Kush, whose Meroë pyramids still stand. The fusion of Arab and African civilizations gives it a distinctive and profound cultural character.
music: Sudanese music is built on the "makam" system, blending Nubian tradition with Arab melody; Mohammed Wardi is hailed as the father of Sudanese music, his voice, at once defiant and heartfelt, influencing a generation of Arabs. Nubian drumming and wedding choral singing are equally moving.

musicians.name: Mohammed Wardi
musicians.desc: The father of Sudanese music and a symbol of the Nubian voice.

radios.name: Sudan Radio
radios.note: The national broadcaster of Sudan.

nigeria.name: Nigeria
nigeria.intro: The birthplace of Afrobeat, where Fela Kuti's rhythm and today's Afrobeats sweep the globe.
history: Nigeria is the most populous country in Africa; hundreds of ethnic groups including the Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo together form its rich cultural landscape. Since the 20th century it has been an engine of African music, literature and cinema (Nollywood).
music: Nigeria is the heart of African popular music: Fela Kuti created Afrobeat in Lagos, fusing high-energy rhythm, funk and political protest; in addition, the Yoruba "Jùjú" and the Igbo "Highlife" are equally influential. Today, Burna Boy, Wizkid and others have made "Afrobeats" a global phenomenon.

musicians.name: Fela Kuti
musicians.desc: The creator of Afrobeat and a revolutionary of African music.

musicians.name: King Sunny Ade
musicians.desc: A master of Yoruba "Jùjú" music.

musicians.name: Burna Boy
musicians.desc: A global standard-bearer of contemporary Afrobeats and a Grammy winner.

radios.name: Cool FM / Rhythm FM Lagos
radios.note: A mainstream music station in Lagos.

ghana.name: Ghana
ghana.intro: The home of Highlife and Hiplife, the elegant source of West African pop.
history: Ghana was one of the first sub-Saharan African countries to gain independence (1957); the gold and cocoa trade of the Ashanti Empire made it prosperous, while the slave forts of Cape Coast recall a heavy history.
music: Ghana is the cradle of Highlife music—an elegant dance music blending local rhythms with Western brass that swept across West Africa, with E.T. Mensah as its founding figure. Contemporary "Hiplife" combines Highlife with hip-hop, carrying on Ghana's pop pulse.

musicians.name: E.T. Mensah
musicians.desc: The "King of Highlife" and founder of modern Ghanaian popular music.

radios.name: Joy FM / Peace FM
radios.note: A mainstream music station in Accra.

senegal.name: Senegal
senegal.intro: The frenetic rhythms of Mbalax and the Dakar sound of Youssou N'Dour.
history: Senegal is a major center of Francophone West African culture; Gorée Island bears witness to the trauma of the slave trade, while Dakar is a vibrant capital of contemporary African art and music.
music: Senegal's signature is "Mbalax," a fast dance music built around the sabar drum, brought to the world by Youssou N'Dour; in addition, the kora singing of the griots and Baaba Maal's Wolof folk songs enjoy international renown.

musicians.name: Youssou N'Dour
musicians.desc: A standard-bearer of Mbalax music and Senegal's most internationally influential voice.

musicians.name: Baaba Maal
musicians.desc: A representative of the fusion of Wolof tradition and modernity.

radios.name: RFM / Zik FM Dakar
radios.note: A mainstream music station in Dakar.

mali.name: Mali
mali.intro: The ancient home of desert blues and the griots, a dialogue between the kora and the guitar.
history: Mali was the core of the Mali Empire and the Songhai Empire, and Timbuktu was once an intellectual capital of the Islamic world. The griots—hereditary bards—remain the custodians of Mali's oral history and music to this day.
music: Mali contributed the legend of desert blues: Ali Farka Touré subtly fused West African tradition with American blues, Salif Keita's "golden voice" is breathtaking, and the duo Amadou & Mariam brought the Malian sound to the world. The kora and the ngoni are its soul instruments.

musicians.name: Ali Farka Touré
musicians.desc: A master of desert blues who fused West African tradition with American blues.

musicians.name: Salif Keita
musicians.desc: The "golden voice" of Mali.

musicians.name: Oumou Sangaré
musicians.desc: The "diva" of Wassoulou music.

radios.name: ORTM Radio Mali
radios.note: The national broadcaster of Mali.

ivory-coast.name: Côte d'Ivoire
ivory-coast.intro: The dance music of Zouglou and Coupé-Décalé, the urban pulse of the Ivory Coast.
history: Côte d'Ivoire (Ivory Coast) is an economic powerhouse of West Africa; Abidjan was once the financial and cultural center of Francophone Africa, and cocoa and coffee built its prosperity.
music: Côte d'Ivoire's contemporary music is full of vitality: "Zouglou" is a protest dance music born on campuses in the 1990s, while "Coupé-Décalé" has swept Francophone Africa with its electronic beats. In reggae, Alpha Blondy is a world-class star.

musicians.name: Alpha Blondy
musicians.desc: The king of African reggae, spreading peace and resistance through music.

radios.name: Radio Côte d'Ivoire
radios.note: The national broadcaster of Côte d'Ivoire.

guinea.name: Guinea
guinea.intro: The kora homeland of Mande music, the deep echo of West African drumming.
history: Guinea was once part of the Mande (Mali) Empire and played an important political role in West Africa after independence. The Fouta Djallon highlands and the source of the Niger River both lie here.
music: Guinea is a major center of Mande music, with deep traditions of the kora, the balafon and the djembe; the national ballet Les Ballets Africains has carried West African drumming to the world. Mory Kanté's "Yéké Yéké" was once a global hit.

musicians.name: Mory Kanté
musicians.desc: The voice behind "Yéké Yéké," who brought Guinean music to the world.

radios.name: Radio Guinée
radios.note: The national broadcaster of Guinea.

burkina-faso.name: Burkina Faso
burkina-faso.intro: The land of the balafon and the griots, the drumming traditions of Ouagadougou.
history: Burkina Faso means "land of upright people" and is a cultural stronghold of the West African interior. The Pan-African Film and Television Festival of Ouagadougou (FESPACO) gives it a prominent place on Africa's cultural map.
music: Burkina Faso's balafon (xylophone) tradition is especially deep, with griot chanting and Mossi drumming as its musical roots; ensembles such as Farafina have carried the sound of this land to the world.

musicians.name: Farafina
musicians.desc: A renowned ensemble combining Burkina Faso's traditional percussion with modern arrangements.

radios.name: Radio Burkina
radios.note: The national broadcaster of Burkina Faso.

niger.name: Niger
niger.intro: The Saharan home of Tuareg blues, the desert guitar sound.
history: Niger is a large landlocked country in West Africa, most of whose territory is the Sahara Desert, where the Tuareg nomads carry on ancient trade routes and culture.
music: Niger is a core of "Tuareg blues": Bombino and Mdou Moctar use electric guitar to express the desolation and freedom of the desert, dubbed the "Jimi Hendrix of the Sahara," astonishing the world with Niger's music.

musicians.name: Bombino
musicians.desc: A standard-bearer of "Tuareg blues," the sound of the Sahara.

musicians.name: Mdou Moctar
musicians.desc: A genius who fuses Tuareg tradition with rock guitar.

radios.name: Voix du Sahel
radios.note: The national broadcaster of Niger.

benin.name: Benin
benin.intro: The rhythms of Vodun and the home of Grammy-winning singer Angélique Kidjo.
history: Benin was the core of the ancient Kingdom of Dahomey, whose Vodun beliefs deeply influenced the religious cultures of the Caribbean and the Americas. The royal palaces of Abomey bear witness to this kingdom's splendor.
music: Benin's music is inseparable from Vodun ritual, with rhythms that are complex and powerful; Angélique Kidjo is Benin's most dazzling international star, a multiple Grammy winner who fuses African music with jazz, funk and Latin.

musicians.name: Angélique Kidjo
musicians.desc: A Grammy winner and the international calling card of Beninese and African music.

radios.name: ORTB Radio
radios.note: The national broadcaster of Benin.

togo.name: Togo
togo.intro: Ewe drum music and the voice of Bella Bellow, a narrow nation on the Gulf of Guinea.
history: Togo is a narrow coastal country in West Africa, with Lomé as its political and economic center; the drumming and oral traditions of the Ewe people are especially rich.
music: Togo's Ewe drum music (such as agbadza) features complex, powerful rhythms and is an important strand of West African percussion; Bella Bellow is Togo's most beloved singer, and her soulful voice is still sung today.

musicians.name: Bella Bellow
musicians.desc: Togo's most representative female singer.

radios.name: Radio Lomé
radios.note: Togo's national broadcaster.

sierra-leone.name: Sierra Leone
sierra-leone.intro: The gentle homeland of palm-wine music and the seaside melodies of Freetown.
history: Freetown in Sierra Leone was one of the earliest settlements of free Black people in West Africa; Creole (Krio) culture blended here, giving rise to a distinctive music and language.
music: Sierra Leone is the birthplace of "palm-wine music" — a relaxed, acoustic-guitar-led style that deeply influenced later highlife and West African pop. S.E. Rogie carried this tradition to the world.

musicians.name: S.E. Rogie
musicians.desc: A representative of palm-wine music, whose warm guitar songs are deeply moving.

radios.name: SLBC Radio
radios.note: Sierra Leone's national broadcaster.

liberia.name: Liberia
liberia.intro: A meeting point of highlife and African-American music, the distinctive soundscape of the West African coast.
history: Liberia is one of Africa's oldest republics, founded by freed American slaves; its flag and institutions were deeply influenced by the United States, while it also retains the rich musical traditions of its indigenous communities.
music: Liberian music blends indigenous African rhythms with American influences, and highlife also has deep roots here; indigenous drumming and choral singing remain vivid in rural festivals.

musicians.name: Liberian Folk Ensemble
musicians.desc: A musical group carrying on Liberia's drumming and highlife traditions.

radios.name: ELBC Radio
radios.note: Liberia's national broadcaster.

gambia.name: The Gambia
gambia.intro: The Mandinka homeland of the kora, a tradition of song along the Gambia River.
history: The Gambia is the smallest country on the African mainland, stretching narrowly along both banks of the Gambia River, where the griot tradition of the Mandinka people has endured for a millennium.
music: The Gambia's kora playing is world-renowned, and the female kora virtuoso Sona Jobarteh is a descendant of a Gambian griot family; Mandinka singing and drumming are equally deep-rooted.

musicians.name: Sona Jobarteh
musicians.desc: The first female kora virtuoso and a descendant of a griot family.

radios.name: GRTS Radio
radios.note: The Gambia's national broadcaster.

guinea-bissau.name: Guinea-Bissau
guinea-bissau.intro: The gumbe rhythms of the Portuguese-speaking West African world, the beat of a tropical coast.
history: Guinea-Bissau is one of the few West African countries with Portuguese as its official language; the tropical scenery of the Bijagós archipelago and its diverse ethnic groups shape its distinctive character.
music: Guinea-Bissau's signature rhythm is "gumbe" — a dance music blending African drumming with Creole elements, and a sound symbol of its national identity; the country's Creole-language songs are also distinctive.

musicians.name: Gumbe Ensemble
musicians.desc: A musical group carrying on the gumbe rhythms of Guinea-Bissau.

radios.name: RDN Radio
radios.note: Guinea-Bissau's national broadcaster.

cape-verde.name: Cape Verde
cape-verde.intro: The melancholy soul of the morna, the island songs of Cesária Évora.
history: Cape Verde is a volcanic archipelago in the Atlantic, once a way station for Portuguese colonization and the slave trade; Creole culture took root here, forming a unique language and music.
music: The soul of Cape Verde is the "morna" — a melancholy, heartfelt ballad inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity; Cesária Évora, singing barefoot, moved audiences around the world with "Sodade". The lively "coladeira" is the archipelago's dance music.

musicians.name: Cesária Évora
musicians.desc: The "Barefoot Diva" who carried Cape Verde's morna to the world.

radios.name: RTC / RCV
radios.note: Cape Verde's national broadcaster.

mauritania.name: Mauritania
mauritania.intro: The deep songs of desert music, the vast soundscape of the Moors and Tuareg.
history: Mauritania straddles West Africa and the Sahara; Moorish culture fused Arab and Berber traditions, and nomadic Tuareg and Hassaniya peoples also make their home here.
music: Mauritania's desert music is profound and delicate; the singer Dimi Mint Abba was hailed as the "Diva of the Desert", and her singing paired with the tidinit string instrument is enchanting; Malouma blends tradition with modernity.

musicians.name: Dimi Mint Abba
musicians.desc: The "Diva of the Desert" and a symbol of Mauritanian music.

radios.name: Radio Mauritanie
radios.note: Mauritania's national broadcaster.

ethiopia.name: Ethiopia
ethiopia.intro: The birthplace of Ethio-jazz, the mysterious sounds of Mulatu Astatke.
history: Ethiopia is the only African empire never to be colonized; the Aksumite civilization, the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, and the castles of Gondar bear witness to three thousand years of independence.
music: The brightest jewel of Ethiopian music is "Ethio-jazz" — Mulatu Astatke fused the Ethiopian pentatonic scale with jazz and funk to create a mysterious, captivating sound; singers such as Mahmoud Ahmed brought Ethiopian pop to its golden age.

musicians.name: Mulatu Astatke
musicians.desc: The "father of Ethio-jazz" and a bridge between jazz and Ethiopian tradition.

musicians.name: Mahmoud Ahmed
musicians.desc: A legendary voice of Ethiopian popular music.

radios.name: Fana FM / Sheger FM
radios.note: Leading stations in Addis Ababa.

kenya.name: Kenya
kenya.intro: Benga guitar music and Swahili pop, the rhythmic capital of East Africa.
history: Kenya is East Africa's economic and cultural center, and Nairobi hosts the UN's African headquarters. The Swahili language links the East African coast into a single cultural world, where music, language, and trade meet from Mombasa to the interior.
music: Kenya's signature is "benga" — dance music built on skipping guitar melodies that swept across East Africa; Swahili pop (such as the coastal variant of taarab) and contemporary "kapuka" are also popular among the young.

musicians.name: Fadhili William
musicians.desc: One of the pioneers of benga music, whose "Malaika" became a Swahili classic.

radios.name: Radio Citizen / Kiss FM
radios.note: Leading music stations in Nairobi.

tanzania.name: Tanzania
tanzania.intro: The Zanzibari flavor of taarab and contemporary Bongo Flava.
history: Tanzania was formed by the union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar, and Swahili spread from here across East Africa. The Stone Town of Zanzibar blends a millennium of Arab, Indian, and African civilization.
music: Tanzania's "taarab" is the signature of the coast — refined music combining Arab melodies with Swahili poetry, and Zanzibar's taarab is inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity; contemporary "Bongo Flava" is East Africa's most popular hip-hop and R&B style.

musicians.name: Bi Kidude
musicians.desc: Zanzibar's "mother of taarab" and a legendary female singer.

radios.name: Clouds FM / Radio One
radios.note: Leading stations in Dar es Salaam.

uganda.name: Uganda
uganda.intro: A fertile ground of East African rhythm, Geoffrey Oryema's voice of Kampala.
history: Uganda is the "Pearl of Africa", where Lake Victoria and the source of the Nile meet; ancient kingdoms such as Buganda left behind rich musical and court traditions.
music: Uganda's musical traditions are diverse: court drumming, East African pop rhythms, and the contemporary narrative songs of "Kadongo Kamu" coexist; Geoffrey Oryema blended Ugandan folk with Western music to win international acclaim.

musicians.name: Geoffrey Oryema
musicians.desc: A musician who carried Ugandan folk music to the world.

radios.name: Radio Simba / Capital FM
radios.note: Leading stations in Kampala.

rwanda.name: Rwanda
rwanda.intro: The drumming tradition of the land of a thousand hills, a sound of harmony reborn from trauma.
history: Rwanda is known as the "land of a thousand hills"; the 1994 genocide was its profound trauma, after which the country rebuilt at astonishing speed, and Kigali became one of Africa's cleanest and most orderly cities.
music: Rwanda's traditional drumming (ingoma) once served the royal court and rituals, with drummers performing complex rhythms with great skill; contemporary Rwandan pop blends East African rhythms with modern production to become the sound of youth culture.

musicians.name: Ingoma Ensemble
musicians.desc: A musical group carrying on Rwanda's court drumming tradition.

radios.name: Radio Rwanda
radios.note: Rwanda's national broadcaster.

burundi.name: Burundi
burundi.intro: The astonishing rhythms of the royal drums (ingoma), inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
history: Burundi is a small highland country in East Africa, famous for its royal drummers (ingoma) and their astonishing collective drumming, whose rhythms once inspired Western musicians.
music: Burundi's royal drums (ingoma) are its proudest cultural heritage — drummers balance huge drums on their heads while dancing and beating out rhythms of breathtaking precision and power, inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

musicians.name: The Royal Drummers of Burundi
musicians.desc: Renowned worldwide for collective drumming with massive drums balanced on their heads.

radios.name: RTNB Radio
radios.note: Burundi's national broadcaster.

somalia.name: Somalia
somalia.intro: Poetry and song of the Horn of Africa, the chanting tradition of a nomadic people.
history: Somalia sits on the "Horn of Africa", an ancient meeting point of nomadic culture and maritime trade, where Mogadishu was once an important port on the Indian Ocean trade routes.
music: Somali music is centered on poetry and chanting, with the oud, drums, and unison chorus at the heart of celebrations; singers such as Maryam Mursal have carried the Somali sound to the world.

musicians.name: Maryam Mursal
musicians.desc: Somalia's most representative female singer.

radios.name: Radio Mogadishu
radios.note: Somalia's national broadcaster.

djibouti.name: Djibouti
djibouti.intro: The Afar and Somali soundscape at the gateway to the Red Sea, a crossroads of the Horn of Africa.
history: Djibouti commands the Bab-el-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea, a strategic point on the Horn of Africa where Afar and Somali communities meet.
music: Djibouti's music blends Afar, Somali, and Arab traditions; nomadic chanting and drumming form its foundation, while the sea breezes of the Indian Ocean lend it a Swahili flavor.

musicians.name: Afar Ensemble
musicians.desc: A musical group carrying on the nomadic chanting tradition of the Afar people.

radios.name: RTD Radio
radios.note: Djibouti's national broadcaster.

eritrea.name: Eritrea
eritrea.intro: A diverse soundscape on the Red Sea shore, where Tigrinya and Arab music meet.
history: Eritrea lies on the western shore of the Red Sea; Asmara preserves elegant Italian colonial architecture, and Tigrinya, Tigre, and Arab cultures intertwine here.
music: Eritrean music blends Tigrinya traditions, Ethiopian scales, and Arab melodies; the krar string instrument and drums are central to celebrations, and its pop music has a wide audience across East Africa.

musicians.name: Eritrean Folk Ensemble
musicians.desc: A group carrying on the Tigrinya musical tradition.

radios.name: Eri-TV Radio
radios.note: Eritrea's national broadcaster.

south-sudan.name: South Sudan
south-sudan.intro: Dinka chanting on the upper Nile, the sound of Africa's youngest nation.
history: South Sudan, which gained independence in 2011, is the world's youngest country; the wetlands of the upper Nile and the pastoral cultures of the Dinka, Nuer, and other peoples form its foundation.
music: South Sudanese music centers on the chanting and drumming of the Dinka, Nuer, and other peoples, with cattle and rivers as eternal themes in song; despite its youth and turbulence, its oral music traditions remain resilient.

musicians.name: South Sudanese Folk Choir
musicians.desc: Carrying on South Sudanese traditions through Dinka chanting and harmony.

radios.name: SSBC Radio
radios.note: South Sudan's national broadcaster.

seychelles.name: Seychelles
seychelles.intro: The sega and moutia of the Indian Ocean, the Creole melodies of a tropical archipelago.
history: Seychelles is a nation of 115 islands in the Indian Ocean; its Creole culture blends African, European, and Asian heritage, and Victoria is Africa's smallest capital.
music: Seychelles' music is marked by the "sega" and the "moutia" — the former a light Creole dance music, the latter rooted in African ritual dance, with passionate rhythms; musicians such as Jean-Marc Volcy have spread the archipelago's sound far and wide.

musicians.name: Jean-Marc Volcy
musicians.desc: One of Seychelles' most representative musicians.

radios.name: SBC Radio
radios.note: Seychelles' national broadcaster.

comoros.name: Comoros
comoros.intro: The Arab-African melodies of the "Moon Islands", the spiced soundscape of the Indian Ocean.
history: The Comoros, known as the "Moon Islands", lie at the northern end of the Mozambique Channel, where Arab, African, and Indian Ocean spice trade have met for a millennium.
music: Comorian music blends Arab maqam with Swahili and Malagasy elements; the drumming, strings, and unison chanting of weddings and religious festivals are its hallmark.

musicians.name: Comorian Ensemble
musicians.desc: A traditional group carrying on Comoros' Arab-African fusion music.

radios.name: ORTC Radio
radios.note: The Comoros' national broadcaster.

madagascar.name: Madagascar
madagascar.intro: The fast rhythms of salegy, the distinctive soundscape of a great Indian Ocean island.
history: Madagascar is the world's fourth-largest island, its culture blending Southeast Asian, African, and Arab heritage; lemurs and baobab trees form a unique natural and cultural landscape.
music: Madagascar's music is extraordinarily distinctive: the rapid "salegy" dance music, the southern "tsapiky" guitar music, and the clear tones of the "valiha" (tube zither) all set this great island's sound apart.

musicians.name: Jaojoby
musicians.desc: The "King of Salegy" and Madagascar's most famous musician.

radios.name: Radio Antsiva
radios.note: A leading station in Antananarivo.

mauritius.name: Mauritius
mauritius.intro: The Creole beat of sega, a multicultural melting pot of the Indian Ocean.
history: Mauritius is a multicultural island nation in the Indian Ocean where people of Indian, African, Chinese, and Creole descent live in harmony, and Port Louis bears witness to the history of colonial trade.
music: Mauritius' signature is the "sega" — Creole dance music featuring the ravanne hand drum, inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity; Kaya (Joseph Réginald Topize) carried the sound of Mauritius to the world.

musicians.name: Kaya (Joseph Réginald Topize)
musicians.desc: A leading figure of Mauritian sega music.

radios.name: MBC Radio
radios.note: Mauritius' national broadcaster.

cameroon.name: Cameroon
cameroon.intro: The dance music of makossa and bikutsi, and Manu Dibango's African funk.
history: Cameroon is called "Africa in miniature"; its diverse geography and ethnic groups condense the richness of an entire continent, with French- and English-speaking regions side by side.
music: Cameroon's "makossa" is one of Africa's most famous dance styles, and Manu Dibango's "Soul Makossa" even influenced funk and disco; the rapid rhythms of "bikutsi" and the bass of Richard Bona are also internationally renowned.

musicians.name: Manu Dibango
musicians.desc: A Cameroonian legend whose "Soul Makossa" influenced global popular music.

musicians.name: Richard Bona
musicians.desc: A world-class bass virtuoso and a bridge between jazz and African music.

radios.name: CRTV Radio
radios.note: Cameroon's national broadcaster.

dr-congo.name: DR Congo
dr-congo.intro: The birthplace of Congolese rumba and soukous, a melting pot of African popular music.
history: The Democratic Republic of the Congo is Africa's second-largest country by area; the Congo River nourishes the world's second-largest tropical rainforest, and Kinshasa and Lubumbashi are major centers of African music.
music: The DR Congo is a powerhouse of African popular music: "Congolese rumba" and "soukous", with their flowing rhythms and agile guitar work, swept across Africa and even Latin America and are inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity; masters such as Franco and Tabu Ley shaped the golden age of African music.

musicians.name: Franco (Luambo Makiadi)
musicians.desc: A giant of Congolese rumba whose band OK Jazz defined African popular music.

musicians.name: Tabu Ley Rochereau
musicians.desc: A legendary singer of Congolese rumba and soukous.

radios.name: RTNC / Top Congo FM
radios.note: Leading stations in Kinshasa.

congo.name: Congo
congo.intro: The other half of Congolese rumba's homeland, the riverside melodies of Brazzaville.
history: The Republic of the Congo faces the DR Congo across the Congo River; Brazzaville and Kinshasa are the two closest capital cities in the world, and the two countries share the lineage of rumba music.
music: The Republic of the Congo, together with its neighbor across the river, gave birth to "Congolese rumba"; Brazzaville's bands are equally prolific, and the melodies of rumba and soukous echo along both banks of the great river.

musicians.name: Congolese Rumba Ensemble
musicians.desc: A musical group carrying on the rumba tradition of both banks of the Congo River.

radios.name: Radio Congo
radios.note: The Republic of the Congo's national broadcaster.

gabon.name: Gabon
gabon.intro: The rhythms of the equatorial rainforest, Pierre Akendengué's voice of Gabon.
history: Gabon straddles the equator, with most of its territory covered by tropical rainforest; its oil resources make it one of the more prosperous countries in Central Africa, and Libreville is a francophone African metropolis.
music: Gabon's music is closely tied to the ritual traditions of the rainforest, with drumming and polyphonic choral singing as its hallmark; Pierre Akendengué blended Gabonese tradition with French chanson to win international acclaim.

musicians.name: Pierre Akendengué
musicians.desc: Gabon's most representative musician.

radios.name: Gabon 1ère
radios.note: Gabon's national broadcaster.

central-african-republic.name: Central African Republic
central-african-republic.intro: Sango chanting and drumming, the oral tradition of the Central African interior.
history: The Central African Republic lies at the geographic center of the African continent; Sango is its lingua franca, and its rainforest and savanna have nurtured rich oral music traditions.
music: Central African music centers on Sango-language chanting, drumming, and the xylophone, with griot-like narrative traditions still alive; despite years of upheaval, its music remains a force for community cohesion.

musicians.name: Central African Ensemble
musicians.desc: A group carrying on the Sango chanting and drumming tradition.

radios.name: Radio Centrafrique
radios.note: The Central African Republic's national broadcaster.

chad.name: Chad
chad.intro: A soundscape on the southern edge of the Sahara, where Arab and African traditions meet.
history: Chad straddles the Sahara and the Sahel; it was once an important node on ancient Saharan trade routes, where Arab and sub-Saharan cultures meet.
music: Chad's music blends Arab maqam with sub-Saharan rhythms; drumming, strings, and chanting are central to its festivals, and the musical traditions of its many ethnic groups are extraordinarily rich.

musicians.name: Chadian Ensemble
musicians.desc: A group carrying on the musical traditions of Chad's diverse ethnic groups.

radios.name: ONRTV Radio
radios.note: Chad's national broadcaster.

equatorial-guinea.name: Equatorial Guinea
equatorial-guinea.intro: Africa's only Spanish-speaking country, a diverse soundscape of the Gulf of Guinea.
history: Equatorial Guinea is the only African country with Spanish as its official language, made up of a mainland region and islands such as Bioko; its oil resources make it one of Africa's higher-income countries per capita.
music: Equatorial Guinean music blends the Spanish colonial legacy with the traditions of the Fang, Bubi, and other peoples, with drumming and guitar songs at the heart of its celebrations.

musicians.name: Equatoguinean Ensemble
musicians.desc: A group carrying on Fang drumming and Spanish-African fusion music.

radios.name: Radio Nacional
radios.note: Equatorial Guinea's national broadcaster.

sao-tome.name: São Tomé and Príncipe
sao-tome.intro: The Creole melodies of a small Gulf of Guinea island, Africa's Portuguese-speaking pearl.
history: São Tomé and Príncipe are two volcanic islands in the Gulf of Guinea, once a Portuguese colony, whose Creole culture is closely tied to the history of coffee and cocoa plantations.
music: São Tomé's music features the "tchiloli" theater and the "socopé" dance, blending African rhythms with Portuguese heritage in a style that is light and passionate.

musicians.name: São Toméan Ensemble
musicians.desc: A group carrying on São Tomé's Creole music.

radios.name: RTP África
radios.note: A Portuguese-language African station covering São Tomé.

angola.name: Angola
angola.intro: A land of semba, kizomba, and kuduro dance music.
history: Angola is the largest Portuguese-speaking African country, rich in oil and quickly rebuilt after a long civil war; Luanda is one of Africa's most bustling metropolises.
music: Angola has contributed some of Africa's most influential dance music: "semba", the romantic "kizomba", and the electronic "kuduro" have all swept the Lusophone world and beyond; Bonga is a legend of Angolan music.

musicians.name: Bonga
musicians.desc: A legendary voice of Angolan semba and folk music.

radios.name: RNA / Luanda Antena
radios.note: Leading stations in Luanda.

south-africa.name: South Africa
south-africa.intro: Isicathamiya harmony and South African jazz, Miriam Makeba's "Rainbow Nation".
history: South Africa is the "Rainbow Nation", where diverse peoples and cultures coexist; from the suffering of apartheid to Mandela's forgiveness, it wrote one of modern history's most moving chapters of reconciliation.
music: South Africa's music is extraordinarily rich: the Zulu "isicathamiya" unaccompanied male choral singing is gentle and harmonious, made world-famous by Ladysmith Black Mambazo; in jazz, Miriam Makeba and Hugh Masekela carried the South African sound across the globe; the Zulu chorus of "The Lion King" spread South African harmony worldwide.

musicians.name: Miriam Makeba
musicians.desc: "Mama Africa", who carried South African music and the anti-apartheid struggle to the world.

musicians.name: Hugh Masekela
musicians.desc: A leading figure of South African jazz.

musicians.name: Ladysmith Black Mambazo
musicians.desc: A legendary Zulu a cappella choir and multiple Grammy winner.

radios.name: Metro FM / SAfm
radios.note: Leading South African music stations.

namibia.name: Namibia
namibia.intro: The ancient soundscape of the Namib Desert and the Khoisan, a vast land of southern Africa.
history: Namibia is famed for the magnificent Namib Desert and the Skeleton Coast; once a German colony, its diverse peoples (Ovambo, Herero, Khoisan, and others) have preserved rich musical traditions.
music: Namibia's music blends Ovambo choral singing, Herero chanting, and the ancient rhythms of the Khoisan; its post-independence pop has drawn on diverse South African and German influences.

musicians.name: Namibian Ensemble
musicians.desc: A group carrying on the musical traditions of Namibia's diverse peoples.

radios.name: NBC Radio
radios.note: Namibia's national broadcaster.

botswana.name: Botswana
botswana.intro: The Tswana soundscape of the Okavango Delta, an oasis of stability and prosperity in Africa.
history: Botswana is one of Africa's most stable and prosperous countries; the Okavango Delta is one of the most unique wetland ecosystems on Earth, and the music and dance traditions of the Tswana people run deep.
music: Botswana's music centers on Tswana choral singing, drumming, and strings; traditional dances such as the setapa have lively rhythms and are important symbols of cultural identity.

musicians.name: Tswana Choir
musicians.desc: A group carrying on Tswana harmony and dance traditions.

radios.name: RB1 / Duma FM
radios.note: Leading stations in Gaborone.

lesotho.name: Lesotho
lesotho.intro: The Sesotho harmony of the "Kingdom in the Sky", a mountainous country encircled by South Africa.
history: Lesotho is the only country in the world whose entire territory lies above 1,000 meters in elevation, known as the "Kingdom in the Sky" and completely surrounded by South Africa.
music: Lesotho's music is dominated by Sesotho choral singing and strings; the distinctive "makorolo" and chanting traditions echo through the mountains, with warm, moving harmonies.

musicians.name: Sesotho Choir
musicians.desc: A group carrying on the Sesotho harmony tradition.

radios.name: Radio Lesotho
radios.note: Lesotho's national broadcaster.

eswatini.name: Eswatini
eswatini.intro: The ritual drumming of the Swazi kingdom, one of Africa's last absolute monarchies.
history: Eswatini (formerly Swaziland) is one of the few African countries retaining an absolute monarchy; Swazi traditional ceremonies (such as the Reed Dance) remain central to its culture.
music: Eswatini's music is inseparable from royal ceremonies, with drumming, chanting, and dance playing a central role in festivals; Swazi traditional songs are the sound of its national identity.

musicians.name: Swazi Ceremonial Ensemble
musicians.desc: A group carrying on the ritual music tradition of the Swazi royal court.

radios.name: EBIS Radio
radios.note: Eswatini's national broadcaster.

zimbabwe.name: Zimbabwe
zimbabwe.intro: The homeland of the mbira thumb piano, the soulful sound of Shona music.
history: Zimbabwe is famed for the stone ruins of "Great Zimbabwe", the heartland of the Shona civilization, and the thunder of Victoria Falls is its natural symbol.
music: Zimbabwe's most precious musical heritage is the "mbira" — a thumb piano with metal keys whose ethereal, cyclical melodies lie at the heart of Shona religion and ritual; Thomas Mapfumo fused Shona tradition with pop to become the voice of the nation.

musicians.name: Thomas Mapfumo
musicians.desc: A pioneer who brought the mbira and Shona tradition into modern popular music.

musicians.name: Oliver Mtukudzi
musicians.desc: One of Zimbabwe's most beloved singers.

radios.name: ZBC Radio / Star FM
radios.note: Leading stations in Harare.

zambia.name: Zambia
zambia.intro: Rhythms along the Zambezi, the diverse soundscape of the Bemba and Ngoni.
history: Zambia is famed for Victoria Falls (Mosi-oa-Tunya) and the Zambezi River; formerly Northern Rhodesia, it is home to the Bemba, Ngoni, and many other peoples.
music: Zambian music centers on the drumming, chanting, and dance of the Bemba, Ngoni, and other peoples; the contemporary "Zamrock" rock scene once flourished as well, a unique chapter of African music.

musicians.name: Zambian Ensemble
musicians.desc: A group carrying on the Bemba and Ngoni musical traditions.

radios.name: ZNBC Radio
radios.note: Zambia's national broadcaster.

malawi.name: Malawi
malawi.intro: The chanting of the "Warm Heart of Africa", rhythms along Lake Malawi.
history: Malawi is famed for the long, narrow Lake Malawi and is known as the "Warm Heart of Africa"; the culture of the Chewa people (such as the Gule Wamkulu masked dance) is inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
music: Malawi's music is marked by Chewa drumming, chanting, and masked dances; the fishing songs of the lake region and village choruses are warm and moving, and contemporary pop also draws on South African and East African influences.

musicians.name: Gule Wamkulu Ensemble
musicians.desc: A group carrying on the music of Malawi's Gule Wamkulu masked dance.

radios.name: MBC Radio
radios.note: Malawi's national broadcaster.

mozambique.name: Mozambique
mozambique.intro: The dance music of marrabenta, the beat of the Portuguese-speaking Indian Ocean coast.
history: Mozambique is a Portuguese-speaking country on the Indian Ocean; Maputo was an important port in the colonial era, and its music blends African, Portuguese, and Indian Ocean influences.
music: Mozambique's signature is "marrabenta" — a cheerful urban dance music and a sound symbol of its national identity; traditional drumming and choral singing also remain vivid in rural festivals.

musicians.name: Marrabenta Ensemble
musicians.desc: A musical group carrying on Mozambique's marrabenta dance music.

radios.name: RM Radio
radios.note: A leading station in Maputo.
